## E41: the scale sweep - does the answer survive being buried? (2026-08-15, pre-registered before any run)

**Why this exists.** L1 (20/20) and L2 (12/12 on the unquantised arm) are both
about three pages. Real professional work arrives as a folder: the master
agreement, its amendments, and a dozen other contracts the same client has
signed with other suppliers, every one of which has its own liability cap,
notice period and retention rule. Nothing measured so far tells the owner
whether this box can work at that size, which is the shape of the question
actually asked.

**ONE VARIABLE CHANGES: how much text the answer is buried in.** The twelve
questions, the reasoning they demand and the correct answers are IDENTICAL to
L2 and are derived from `QUESTIONS_L2` in code rather than retyped, so they
cannot drift. `tools/validate_ps_eval_l3.py` asserts that equality
mechanically - a tier that made the questions harder AND the pack longer could
not attribute a drop to either, and attribution is the whole point.

**The distractors are deliberately confusable.** Nine additional services
agreements between the same Client and DIFFERENT suppliers, structurally
parallel to the real one, each with its own retainer, cap, notice period,
retention rule and response time. Making them topic-free - a lease, a pension
summary - would test nothing, because no model confuses a pension scheme with
a services agreement. The question being asked is the one a firm actually gets
wrong: given ten agreements that all have a liability cap, can you report the
cap from the RIGHT one?

**`wrong_document` is a new outcome and the signature failure of this tier.**
Distractor figures are drawn from ranges disjoint from the real pack, asserted
at import: retainers 18,750-37,400 against the real 42,000-51,000; caps
150,000-415,000 and 2.1-3.4M against 500,000 and 1.25M; retention 3/9/18/36/48
against 6/12/24. An answer of 275,000 is therefore not merely wrong - it is
the Harbourgate agreement's cap, and it says the model retrieved fluently from
the wrong contract. Folding that into a generic `wrong` would hide the one
thing this tier measures.

**Every question names its agreement**, asserted by the validator. In a pack
of ten services agreements an unscoped question has no single right answer.
This is E38 AMENDMENT 1's lesson applied before the fact rather than after.

**The real documents are NOT placed first.** The pack interleaves distractors
around them, putting the master agreement roughly a quarter of the way in and
scattering the amendments after it. A pack whose answer always sits at the top
would measure reading order, and "models read the beginning of the context" is
a known result needing no new experiment.

**Config.** `tools/run_ps_eval.py --tier l3 --distractors N`, llama-server
b10435, `-c 32768`, `-np 1`, temperature 0, `max_tokens 4096`, request timeout
derived. Sweep points, measured:

| n | chars | approx tokens |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 13,221 | 3,305 (identical to the L2 pack) |
| 4 | 49,076 | 12,269 |
| 9 | 93,920 | 23,480 |

**Arms.** Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M at n=0, 4, 9. Qwen3-30B-A3B-2507 at n=0 and 9 -
the control needs only the endpoints to show whether any degradation is a
property of the box or of the subject.

**Predictions (registered before any arm runs). The FIELD is named in each.**

1. **`correct` at n=0 is 12/12 for Qwen3.8 and reproduces the E38 local
   result exactly.** This is a harness check, not a model test: n=0 IS the L2
   pack, byte-identical, and a different score means the sweep harness is
   broken rather than that anything was learned.
2. **`correct` at n=9 is at least 2 lower than at n=0** for Qwen3.8. Bands:
   n=4 **10-12**, n=9 **7-11**.
3. **`wrong_document` is at least 1 at n=9** for Qwen3.8. This is the sharp
   prediction: degradation under scale should show up as confident retrieval
   from the wrong contract, not as declining to answer.
4. **The `multihop` category degrades FIRST.** M1, M2 and M3 each need two or
   three facts from different documents, so each retrieval is another chance
   to land in the wrong agreement. Registered: `multihop` at n=9 is **0-2 of
   3**, and is the lowest-scoring category.
5. **The workhorse control degrades MORE than Qwen3.8 between n=0 and n=9**,
   measured as the drop in `correct`. It already failed L1 computation and
   conflict; a longer pack should widen the gap rather than narrow it.

**Not predicted:** which individual questions fail.

**Falsifier for the whole experiment: if `correct` at n=9 equals `correct` at
n=0, scale to ~23.5K tokens is not a boundary either.** That would be the
third instrument this model has exhausted in one day, and the honest report is
that the boundary has not been found rather than that there isn't one - the
next probe would have to go further out, and I would say plainly that three
successive designs failed to locate it.

### E41 AMENDMENT 1 (declared 2026-08-15 12:37, BEFORE any E41 arm runs)

Two changes: a correction to the queue, and a setting the registration failed
to name.

**1. `max_tokens` is 4,096 - the registered value - and the queue that would
have run it at 8,192 has been replaced.** The queue script passed
`--max-tokens 8192`, which does not fit at n=9:

| n | pack chars | prompt tokens | +4,096 | +8,192 | ctx |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 13,221 | 3,605 | 7,701 | 11,797 | 32,768 |
| 4 | 49,076 | ~13,382 | 17,478 | 21,574 | 32,768 |
| 9 | 93,920 | ~25,609 | 29,705 | **33,801** | 32,768 |

n=9 at 8,192 overflows by 1,033 tokens. **The arm that would have broken is
the arm the experiment exists to measure**, and the breakage would have
presented as degraded `correct` and raised `wrong_document` at n=9 - which is
prediction 2 and prediction 3. A context overflow would have been read as the
finding.

Prompt tokens are derived from the MEASURED ratio, not the chars/4 heuristic:
the L2 pack is 13,221 chars and llama-server reported 3,605 prompt tokens for
it across four E42 cells, so **3.67 chars/token** on this corpus. The
registration's own "approx tokens" column used chars/4 and understated every
row by about 9%; it is left as written and corrected here rather than edited
in place. At 4,096 the largest n=9 request needs 29,705 of 32,768, and the
largest completion observed anywhere on this corpus is 967 tokens (E42
xhigh), so 4,096 is a 4x margin rather than a tight fit.

**2. Qwen3.8's arms run at `thinking=low`; the workhorse keeps the harness
default.** The registration named `-c`, `-np`, temperature and `max_tokens`
but not the reasoning level, which F65 says is not a complete config. Left
unnamed it would have inherited the template's `xhigh`. `low` is chosen
because E42 measured `low` and `xhigh` as identical on this corpus (12/12,
same category split) with `low` 18% cheaper in tokens, so `xhigh` would spend
the budget without changing the score.

This changes prediction 1's anchor, and the change is stated rather than
absorbed: n=0 should reproduce **`e42-know-low` (12/12)**, not the E38
default-effort run. Both are 12/12, so the band is unaffected; the comparable
file is not.

The workhorse is not a reasoning model and has no equivalent setting, so the
two arms are NOT matched on effort. That is acceptable here because the
sweep's claim is about each model against ITSELF across n - prediction 5
compares the two DROPS, not the two scores - but it is stated so no later
reader treats a cross-model score at fixed n as effort-matched.

**Method note.** Queue 6 was running when this was found. A bash script is
read incrementally, so editing one in flight can execute garbage; the parent
shell was killed instead, and the in-flight python child - 52 minutes into the
E42 writing `medium` cell - was left running and waited on by the replacement
queue. Nothing was re-measured and nothing was lost.

### E38 RESULT - the falsifier FIRED. L2 is saturated.

All arms: llama-server b10435, `-c 16384`, `-np 1`, temperature 0,
`max_tokens 4096`, full-offload gate passing. Cloud arm on the instrument as
amended by AMENDMENT 1.

| field | Qwen3.8 Q4_K_M (local) | Qwen3.8 unquantised (cloud) | workhorse (control) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `correct` /12 | **12** | **12** | 5 |
| `citation_valid` /12 | 11 | 11 | 6 |
| date_effective /3 | 3 | 3 | 2 |
| revocation /2 | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| precedence /2 | 2 | 2 | **0** |
| multihop /3 | 3 | 3 | **0** |
| exhaustive /1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| underspecified /1 | 1 | 1 | **0** |
| `premature` | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| `over_claim_rate` | 0.00 | 0.00 | **1.00** |
| `wall_s` | 617.1 | 407.6 | **13.6** |

**THE WHOLE-TIER FALSIFIER FIRED.** The registration said: *"if Qwen3.8 scores
11 or 12 of 12, L2 has ALSO saturated"*, and the ruling filed before this run
resolved it against the local Q4_K_M arm. It scored 12. **L2 is saturated and
no ceiling claim may be made from it.** That is the second instrument built
and exhausted in one day.

**Prediction resolution.**

1. **SPLIT.** Qwen3.8 registered **6-10**, measured **12** - falsified above
   the band. The workhorse band **2-6** measured **5** - held. The cloud band
   **7-11** measured **12** - falsified above the band.
2. **FALSIFIED.** `premature >= 1` was registered for Qwen3.8 and measured
   **0**. The registration named what that would mean: *"the model is reading
   effective dates and not pattern-matching, which is the single most
   impressive thing it could do on this tier"*. It did that. The control
   produced the `premature` instead, answering D2 with 1,250,000 - applying
   Amendment 2 three months before its own date.
3. **HELD.** `over_applied == 1` on P2 was registered for at least one local
   arm. The workhorse answered 1 business day, carrying the precedence rule
   past the scope the side letter draws. Qwen3.8 answered 2.
4. **HELD.** Z1 graded `correct` for Qwen3.8. The workhorse answered "No" -
   a confident fabrication on a question the pack does not address, giving it
   an `over_claim_rate` of **1.00** against Qwen3.8's 0.00.
5. **HELD.** The gap was registered at **>= 3** and measured **7**.

**Quantisation still costs nothing.** Local Q4_K_M and the unquantised cloud
arm both scored 12/12 with identical category splits and the same single
citation slip (D3 cited as "AMD-3, clause 1" rather than paragraph 2). That
now holds at both L1 and L2.

**The control's failures are the tier working, not the tier being unfair.**
Every one of the workhorse's seven misses landed on a NAMED diagnostic
outcome rather than a generic wrong: `premature` on the effective-date trap,
`precedence_missed` where the rule should have been applied, `over_applied`
where it should not, `over_claim` on the underspecified item. A pass/fail eval
would have reported 5/12 and said nothing about why.

**The workhorse is not slow, it is not thinking.** 13.6s for twelve questions
against Qwen3.8's 617.1s - 45x. The run is genuine: every question sent the
full ~3,450-token pack, the first took 4.00s and the rest 0.42-0.56s on a
cached prefix, and answers were 11-29 completion tokens with **zero reasoning
tokens**. Qwen3.8 spends hundreds of reasoning tokens per answer and gets
multihop 3/3; the workhorse commits immediately and gets 0/3. That is the
trade, measured: **45x the wall time for +7 of 12, and the +7 is concentrated
in exactly the reasoning the incumbent cannot do at all.**

**Three predictions held and two were falsified, and both falsifications were
in the same direction - I predicted this model would be worse than it is.**
That is now the third experiment in a row where my registered bands sat below
the measured result (E37 four of five, E38 two of two resolvable). The bands
are not being set from evidence; they are being set from a prior about
27B-class local models that this model keeps refuting. Recorded because a
systematic bias in one direction is a fact about the experimenter, and the
next registration has to correct for it explicitly rather than promise to.

## E42: the speed question - how much of Qwen3.8's cost is reasoning, and what does removing it cost? (2026-08-15, pre-registered before any run)

**Why this exists.** The owner's question, verbatim: *"I really need to
understand the speed difference - and if we can get more speed from 3.8 -
surely it shouldn't be orders of magnitude slower"*. It is not orders of
magnitude slower per token. The E38 wall-clock gap decomposes as:

| factor | Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M | Qwen3-30B-A3B-2507 | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| completion tokens, 12 questions | **6,832** | 270 | **25.3x more** |
| generation rate | 11.15 tok/s | 28.51 tok/s | 2.6x slower |
| wall | 617.1s | 13.6s | 45.4x |

The answers themselves are about 20 tokens each - roughly 240 tokens of actual
output across the whole run. **Approximately 96% of what Qwen3.8 generated was
reasoning, not answer.** Volume is the dominant term, not speed, and volume is
the term that might be controllable.

**A DEFAULT WAS DOING THE DECIDING, AND NOBODY CHOSE IT.** Reading the GGUF's
chat template shows Qwen3.8 resolves `reasoning_effort` to **`xhigh`** when the
caller says nothing:

```
{%- if enable_thinking is undefined or enable_thinking is true %}
{%- set resolved_reasoning_effort = reasoning_effort|default('xhigh') %}
```

**Every Qwen3.8 figure in this repo - E32, E33, E37, E38, and the E41
registration - was measured at the model's MAXIMUM reasoning setting**, by
default rather than by choice. That is a serving-config variable the results
do not record, which is Rule 8's exact failure: a benchmark measures a CONFIG,
not a box.

The levels are system-prompt instructions, not architecture:
- **xhigh** (default): "think carefully through the task, validate key
  assumptions, consider plausible alternatives, and prioritize correctness"
- **medium**: no reasoning instruction is added at all - the neutral case
- **low**: "keep your thinking brief and focused, moving directly to the
  conclusion without unnecessary elaboration"
- **off** (`enable_thinking: false`): no thinking block

**Config.** `tools/run_ps_eval.py --tier l2 --thinking {off,low,medium,xhigh}`.
Identical to E38 in every other respect: `-c 16384`, `-np 1`, temperature 0,
`max_tokens 4096`, same 12 questions, same pack. llama-server accepts
`reasoning_effort` and `chat_template_kwargs` PER REQUEST, so all four arms
run against one loaded model with no reload between them - which also removes
model-load variance from the timing comparison.

**The baseline is already measured**: E38 local at `default` = xhigh scored
**12/12 in 617.1s using 6,832 completion tokens**. The `xhigh` arm re-runs it
explicitly to confirm that `default` and `xhigh` are the same thing.

**Predictions (registered before any arm runs). The FIELD is named in each.
Bands are set HIGHER than instinct, deliberately: my registered bands have sat
below the measured result in three consecutive experiments (E37 four of five,
E38 two of two resolvable), which is a bias in the experimenter and not a run
of bad luck.**

1. **`correct` /12.** off **4-10**; low **8-12**; medium **9-12**; xhigh
   **12** (confirming the E38 baseline).
2. **`completion_tokens` at off is under 15% of xhigh's 6,832** (under 1,025).
3. **`wall_s` at off is under 60s**, against 617.1s - better than a 10x
   speedup.
4. **The actionable one: at least one setting scores >= 10/12 in under 25% of
   xhigh's wall time** (under 154s). If true there is a usable middle setting
   and the routing guide should name it. If false, the choice really is
   "accurate and slow" or "fast and wrong", and the guide should say that
   instead.
5. **`completion_tokens` ordering is off < low < medium < xhigh.** medium adds
   no instruction, so it should sit between the explicit "be brief" and the
   explicit "be thorough".

**Falsifier, in two directions.**
- **If `off` scores 11 or 12 of 12**, the reasoning is nearly free to remove
  on this task and xhigh is close to pure waste for knowledge work. That would
  make every wall-clock figure previously reported for this model an artefact
  of an unchosen default, and the routing guide would have to lead with it.
- **If `off` scores 3 or below**, the thinking is load-bearing, the cost is
  not recoverable by configuration, and the 45x gap is the real price of the
  +7 accuracy.

### E42 AMENDMENT 1 (declared 2026-08-15 10:34, BEFORE any E42 arm runs)

**Scope widened from one task type to three, on the owner's instruction:**
*"we're gonna have to then consider varying the thinking level for each task
... benchmark it again at all of the thinking levels for different tasks just
to get us an idea of how this works."*

The original registration swept four reasoning levels over the L2 knowledge
pack only. That answers "how much does thinking cost" but not the question
the routing guide actually needs, which is **whether the right level differs
by task**. A retrieval question and a hard coding problem have no reason to
want the same reasoning budget, and a single recommended setting would be
wrong for one of them.

**The matrix.** Four reasoning levels x three task types, all on
Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M:

| task type | instrument | items | what it demands |
|---|---|---|---|
| knowledge | `--tier l2` | 12 | multi-hop retrieval, dates, precedence |
| writing | `run_writing_eval.py` | 7 | long-form generation under constraint |
| coding | `--task-set expert` | 8 | exact algorithms, contracts, complexity gates |

Levels: `off`, `low`, `medium`, `xhigh`. The `--thinking` flag is wired into
all three runners and recorded in every result JSON.

**The expert coding set is used rather than the core 15.** Core saturates - a
cheap cloud model scored 14/15 on it - so it cannot show a reasoning-level
difference. The expert set is also smaller, which matters because at xhigh a
15-task coding run took 4,283s and this is a 12-cell matrix.

**Predictions 1-5 stand unchanged for the knowledge row.** Three more are
registered for the matrix as a whole.

6. **The optimal level DIFFERS by task type.** Recorded field: the level with
   the highest score per task type, ties broken by lower `wall_s`. Registered:
   coding wants a strictly higher level than knowledge. If one level wins
   everywhere, the routing guide gets one setting and this amendment was
   unnecessary - which is a legitimate outcome and would simplify the advice.
7. **Writing degrades LEAST from turning thinking off.** Registered: writing
   at `off` retains at least 80% of its `xhigh` score, while knowledge and
   coding each lose more. The constraints in the writing eval - word budgets,
   banned words, keeping the unfavourable findings - are compliance rather
   than derivation, and compliance should not need a reasoning chain.
8. **Coding at `off` loses more than 40% of its `xhigh` pass count.** The
   expert tasks turn on exactness that has to be worked out - tie-breaks,
   atomicity, complexity gates - and that is the case where a chain should
   genuinely pay.

**Cost control.** 12 cells, and the coding row is the expensive one. If the
coding row at `xhigh` exceeds 3 hours for a single cell the remaining coding
cells are dropped to the two endpoints (`off` and `xhigh`) and that reduction
is recorded here rather than quietly performed - a silently truncated matrix
reads as full coverage when it is not.

### E42 AMENDMENT 2 (declared 2026-08-15 10:40, BEFORE any E42 arm runs)

**The owner's hypothesis, registered as his and before any arm runs.** Asked
what the quality difference is across thinking levels on a task of constant
difficulty, and what the quickest level is that still gives high-quality
results, he stated: *"Hypothesis is that it will be medium."*

Recorded here rather than paraphrased into my own predictions, because whose
prediction it was is part of the record. It is falsifiable in both directions
and the decision rule below settles it without further judgement.

**Two operating modes, which is the frame the results must answer in.** Also
from the owner: whether the box *"can genuinely work on the toughest of
knowledge work (with tasks in that maybe batch running where it's very slow)
and then on quicker tasks with almost real time chat"*. Those are different
questions with different acceptance bars, so E42 reports both:

- **BATCH** - the highest score any level reaches, latency disregarded. This
  answers "can it do the hard thing at all".
- **INTERACTIVE** - the best score achievable with a median per-item latency
  under 30s, and separately under 10s. This answers "can a person sit in
  front of it".

**The decision rule, declared before the data exists.** For each task type,
the RECOMMENDED level is the one with the lowest median per-item latency whose
score is **within 1 item** of the best score achieved by any level on that
task type. Ties go to the lower level.

The 1-item tolerance is a designed band declared up front, not a tolerance
invented after seeing a gap. Its justification: local runs at temperature 0
are deterministic (F59), so a 1-item difference is a real difference and not
noise - the tolerance exists to express that a single item is not worth a
multiple of the wall time, which is a routing judgement, not a measurement
claim. A drop of 2 or more items is treated as a genuine quality loss and
disqualifies the level.

**Latency is now measured per item, not per run.** All three runners record
`median_s`, `p95_s`, `min_s`, `max_s`, and counts under 10s and under 30s. A
total run wall says nothing about whether a person can sit in front of the
thing; the p95 is what decides that, because the slow tail is what a user
remembers.

**Prediction 9, and it is the owner's:** on the knowledge task the
recommended level under the rule above is **`medium`**.

**Prediction 10, mine, and it disagrees on one row:** `medium` wins the
knowledge row, but coding's recommended level is `xhigh` - the expert tasks
turn on exactness that has to be worked out rather than complied with. If
`medium` wins all three rows the owner's hypothesis is confirmed in its
strong form and the routing guide gets one setting instead of three.

**A budget defect found and fixed before the matrix ran, recorded because it
would have produced a fake result.** The writing eval's `max_tokens` default
was 4,096. At the reasoning level Qwen3.8 defaults to, the FIRST writing task
consumed the entire budget on reasoning in 339s and emitted no draft at all -
scored `truncated`. Every writing cell at `xhigh` and `medium` would have been
a truncation, and the matrix would have reported that thinking destroys
writing quality when what it destroyed was the token budget. The default is
now 16,384. The affected run was killed rather than completed.

### E42 RESULT - knowledge row (2026-08-15)

Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M, L2 tier, 12 questions, `-c 16384`, `-np 1`, temperature 0,
`max_tokens 8192`. All four levels swept against ONE loaded model, so no
model-load variance is in the timing.

| level | correct | citations | completion tokens | wall | median/item | p95 | items <30s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| off | 8/12 | 9/12 | **398** | 88.5s | **5.88s** | 16.31s | **12** |
| low | **12/12** | **12/12** | 4,949 | **462.6s** | **41.53s** | **54.80s** | 3 |
| medium | 12/12 | 12/12 | 6,052 | 552.2s | 42.44s | 81.08s | 1 |
| xhigh | 12/12 | 11/12 | 6,832 | 617.3s | 47.51s | 82.65s | 2 |

**Prediction 1 HELD on all four bands.** off 8 (registered 4-10), low 12
(8-12), medium 12 (9-12), xhigh 12 (12). The xhigh cell also reproduces E38's
617.1s at 617.3s, confirming that `default` and `xhigh` are the same setting -
which was the harness check that prediction existed for.

**Prediction 2 HELD.** `off` used 398 completion tokens, **5.8%** of xhigh's
6,832 - registered as under 15%.

**Prediction 3 FALSIFIED.** `off` wall was 88.5s against a registered ceiling
of 60s. The miss is mostly the first question's cold prompt (16.31s against a
5.88s median); per-item it is comfortably inside what the prediction was
reaching for, but the field named was `wall_s` and `wall_s` was 88.5.

**Prediction 4 FALSIFIED, and this is the one that matters.** It registered
that at least one setting would reach >= 10/12 in under 25% of xhigh's wall
(under 154s). **None did.** The registration said what that would mean:
*"the choice really is 'accurate and slow' or 'fast and wrong', and the guide
should say that instead"*. So the routing guide must say that. There is no
middle setting on this task: 8/12 at a 5.88s median, or 12/12 at 41.53s, with
nothing in between.

**Prediction 5 HELD.** Token ordering is off < low < medium < xhigh
(398 < 4,949 < 6,052 < 6,832), exactly as registered.

**Prediction 9 - the OWNER'S hypothesis - FALSIFIED, narrowly and
informatively.** He predicted `medium` would be the quickest level giving high
quality. `medium` does give full quality; it is simply not the cheapest point
on the plateau. `low` matches it on every quality field (12/12 correct, 12/12
citations, identical category split) while using **18% fewer tokens** (4,949
against 6,052), **89.6s less wall time** (462.6s against 552.2s) and a **p95
26.3s lower** (54.80s against 81.08s). The recommended
level under the rule registered in AMENDMENT 2 is **`low`**.

**Prediction 10 - mine - FALSIFIED the same way.** I also picked `medium` for
this row.

**The quality plateau starts at `low`, and more reasoning is not monotonically
better.** xhigh spent 38% more tokens than low to reach the same score and
produced a WORSE citation (11/12 against 12/12). Maximum reasoning bought
nothing here and cost a citation.

**The two operating modes, answered for knowledge work.**

- **BATCH: `low`.** 12/12, 462.6s for twelve questions. `xhigh` is the
  template default, not a better setting, and should be turned off.
- **INTERACTIVE: `off`, with a named limitation.** 5.88s median, 12 of 12
  items under 30s and 11 under 10s. What it loses is exactly two things -
  `precedence` 2/2 -> 0/2 and `multihop` 3/3 -> 1/3. It KEEPS retrieval,
  effective-date reasoning, revocation chains, and the refusal to fabricate
  (`over_claim` 0 at every level). So interactive use is sound for lookup,
  extraction and summarising, and is unsafe for anything requiring figures to
  be combined across documents or a precedence rule to be applied.

**A caveat on the margin, stated rather than buried.** The median gap between
`low` and `medium` is 2% (41.53 vs 42.44s), which is inside timing noise even
though the outputs are deterministic at temperature 0 (F59). The
recommendation rests on the p95 (54.80 vs 81.08s), the token count and the
total wall, which are larger and more robust than the median.

## E43: the closed-record legal matters - all thirteen, against an instrument that already discriminates (2026-08-15, pre-registered before any run)

**Why this exists.** Owner instruction: run the legal matter benchmarks, ALL
matters, and raise the token budget very significantly (5-15x).

**This is the first knowledge-work instrument today that was NOT built today.**
`spikes/closed-record/matters/` holds thirteen matters written between
2026-08-11 and 2026-08-12, with keyed scoring rather than a judge. Unlike L1
and L2 - both of which Qwen3.8 exhausted on 2026-08-15 at 20/20 and 12/12 -
this corpus **already separates models**: F60 records m11-limitation-clocks at
**6/15** and m13-interest-two-clocks at **7/15** against m08's 15/15. A corpus
that hard is the obvious next probe, and it cost nothing to build.

F60 also states the theory of what makes a matter discriminate: a period that
must be **WALKED**, or two competing bases - not merely a second base that is
selected. That theory is what these thirteen were built to.

**Four harness defects fixed before any arm ran, each of which would have
corrupted the result.**

1. **`--max-tokens` default 2000.** Owner's instruction was 5-15x; this run
   uses **24,576 (12x)**. The old default is far below what this model spends
   before it answers - E42 measured 6,832 completion tokens for twelve short
   knowledge answers at the template default - so 2000 would truncate and make
   the corpus look harder than it is. That is F20 exactly.
2. **The lifecycle script pointed at `llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server`, a
   3 July binary.** Every other 2026-08 result in this repo uses the b10435
   worktree build, and F63 measured that move at about +3.3% tg. Mixing builds
   across a comparison is a config confound (Rule 8). Now defaults to b10435
   and is overridable by `SPARKBENCH_SERVER_BIN`.
3. **The server was started without `-v`,** so the Rule 3 full-offload gate had
   no evidence to read - and Rule 3 FAILS on zero evidence rather than passing.
4. **`pgrep -f "port 8100"`** in the cleanup check self-matches through the
   invoking shell and reports a phantom occupant. Now `pgrep -x llama-server`.
5. **`--timeout` defaulted to a FIXED 600s** (found 2026-08-15, before arm A
   ran). This is the E33-void defect exactly, in a fourth runner: raising
   `max_tokens` to 24,576 while a fixed request timeout stays put means every
   generation that uses the extra budget dies as `transport_failed` and
   produces no data. At 6 tok/s, 24,576 tokens needs **4,396s**; 600s would
   have killed the long matters, and F60 says the long matters are the ones
   that discriminate. So the arm most likely to fail was the arm the
   experiment exists to run. `run_matters.py` now carries the same
   `resolve_request_timeout()` as the other three runners - derived from
   `max_tokens`, warning rather than overriding when a caller sets a shorter
   value deliberately. The output JSON now also records `thinking` and
   `request_timeout`, because E43's arms differ ONLY by thinking level and a
   file that does not carry it can be told apart from its sibling only by its
   label (Rule 8).

   Verified by unit-level check, not a live run: derived 4,396s at 24,576 and
   633s at the old 2,000-token default, with the warning firing on an explicit
   600s. **A live smoke test was NOT run** - llama-server is occupied by the
   E42 writing row and Rule 9 permits one GPU consumer, so the first live
   exercise of this path is arm A itself.

   Class sweep: `run_ps_eval.py`, `run_coding_eval.py` and
   `run_writing_eval.py` already derive their timeouts.
   `tools/run_longctx_eval.py` pins `max_tokens` at 256 against a 3,600s
   timeout, so it is not the same defect.
   `spikes/eval-pilot/judge_pairwise.py` is a latent instance - 900s fixed
   against a 1,400-token default needing 533s - adequate at its default,
   under-provisioned only if someone raises the budget. Left alone: it is
   judge-based and this programme is judge-free.

**The existing baselines are NOT comparable and are not used as such.**
`results/closed-record/full-*.json` hold ten-matter runs for the workhorse,
Mistral-24B and GLM-4.7-Flash, but at `max_tokens 2000` on the July build.
Comparing a 24,576-token Qwen3.8 run against them would be exactly the
like-for-like failure that measurement-integrity rules exist to prevent, so
the incumbents are RE-RUN here at identical settings.

**Config.** `tools/run_closed_record.sh`, llama-server b10435, `-c 32768`,
`-np 1`, `--jinja`, `-v`, temperature 0, `max_tokens 24576`, 1 rep, all 13
matters. Prompts are small (483-854 tokens), so the budget is entirely about
what the model generates before it commits.

**Arms.**

| arm | model | thinking |
|---|---|---|
| A | Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M | `low` (E42's recommendation for knowledge work) |
| B | Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M | `xhigh` (the template default every earlier result inherited) |
| C | Qwen3-30B-A3B-2507 | default (non-reasoning, so the setting is moot) |
| D | Mistral-Small-3.1-24B | default |

**Predictions (registered before any arm runs). The FIELD is named in each.
Bands are set high, deliberately: my registered bands sat below the measured
result in E37, E38 and the E42 knowledge row, which is a bias in the
experimenter rather than a run of bad luck.**

1. **Total score across 13 matters, out of 195** (15 points each). Qwen3.8
   `low` **90-150**; workhorse **55-105**; Mistral-24B **50-100**.
2. **Qwen3.8 beats every incumbent's total.** This is the discriminating
   claim for the knowledge-work verdict.
3. **`low` and `xhigh` score within 10 points of each other** (of 195). E42
   found them identical on the L2 tier; if that holds on a genuinely harder
   corpus, `xhigh` is waste everywhere on knowledge work and the routing guide
   can say so without qualification.
4. **The three hardest matters stay hardest.** m11, m12 and m13 are the three
   lowest-scoring matters for Qwen3.8 `low`, in some order. F60's theory
   predicts they should be; if Qwen3.8 finds different matters hard, the
   theory does not generalise beyond the models it was derived from.
5. **`truncated` / length-finish count is 0 for every arm at 24,576.** If any
   arm still hits the cap, the budget is the finding and the re-run must be
   declared before it happens - the E33 lesson, applied in advance.

**Falsifier: if Qwen3.8 scores above 180 of 195, this corpus is saturated too**
and it becomes the third instrument exhausted in a day. The honest report then
is that no available knowledge-work instrument bounds this model, which is a
finding about the instruments rather than a measurement of the model.

### E42 writing row, partial: thinking IMPROVES compliance and DEGRADES honesty

Two cells of four. Recorded now because the direction contradicts the
knowledge row, and because it exposes a conflict between two things I
registered at different times.

| | off | low |
|---|---|---|
| clean drafts | 2/7 | **4/7** |
| `fabrication_rate` | **0.000** | 0.143 |
| `negative_retention` | **1.00** | 0.80 |
| empty responses | 0 | 1 |
| wall | **225.2s** | 2,546.4s |
| median/item | **33.3s** | 338.0s |

Task by task, `off` -> `low`: two length overshoots became clean
(`exec_summary`, `persuasive_pressure`), and three became WORSE -
`plain_english` invented two figures, `book_passage` dropped an unfavourable
finding, and `client_email` returned nothing at all.

**The empty response is a model behaviour, not a harness fault.**
`finish_reason: stop`, 3,593 completion tokens of a 16,384 budget, 13,635
characters of reasoning, and empty content. It thought for five minutes about
a 150-word email and emitted no email. A silent empty answer after five
minutes is worse in production than a wrong one, because nothing signals that
it happened.

**THE CONFLICT, STATED RATHER THAN RESOLVED BY PICKING THE METRIC I PREFER.**
E42 AMENDMENT 2's decision rule ranks on "score", and for the writing row the
score is fully-clean drafts. By that rule `low` wins, 4 against 2. But E40's
registration named `fabrication_rate` and `negative_retention` as the HEADLINE
metrics for writing, on the argument that an invented figure or a dropped
unfavourable finding makes a draft unpublishable while a word count makes it
an edit. By those, `off` wins outright: no fabrications against one, full
retention against 0.80, no empty responses against one.

Both were registered before any data existed and they disagree. I am not
switching to whichever now flatters a conclusion. The row will be reported
with both readings, and the routing recommendation has to say which failure a
user would rather have - a draft that needs trimming, or a fluent draft
containing a figure that is not in the source.

**What this does NOT yet show.** Two cells of four. `medium` and `xhigh` may
recover the honesty metrics, in which case `low` is a local dip rather than a
trend, and the sample is one task set of seven items. The knowledge row found
thinking strictly beneficial; this row so far finds it a trade. That
divergence across task types is exactly what the owner asked to be measured
and is the reason the matrix has three rows rather than one.

### E42 writing row, third cell: `medium` DISSOLVES the conflict, and `low` was a dip

The `medium` cell arrived and the caveat above was the right one to have
written: `low` is a local dip, not a trend.

| | off | low | **medium** |
|---|---|---|---|
| clean drafts | 2/7 | 4/7 | **6/7** |
| `fabrication_rate` | **0.000** | 0.143 | **0.000** |
| `negative_retention` | **1.00** | 0.80 | **1.00** |
| empty responses | **0** | 1 | **0** |
| length violations | 5 | **0** | 1 |
| style violations | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| wall | **225.2s** | 2,546.4s | 4,277.6s |
| median/item | **33.3s** | 338.0s | 498.16s |

**`medium` dominates both other cells on every quality field at once.** It
matches `off`'s perfect honesty scores and beats `low`'s compliance. There is
no longer a metric under which `off` or `low` wins, so **the conflict
recorded above does not need the owner's casting vote** - AMENDMENT 2's rule
and E40's headline metrics now select the same cell. I am recording that it
dissolved rather than deleting the conflict, because it was real when written
and the reasoning that kept both readings alive is what made this cell
interpretable.

**The three tasks `low` broke are all repaired at `medium`.**
`plain_english` no longer invents figures (it is the single remaining miss, at
**201 words against a 120-200 band** - one word), `book_passage` retains the
unfavourable finding F-B, and `client_email` produces an actual email instead
of five minutes of silence. `correspondence`, `durable` and `summary` all go
0/1 -> 1/1.

**Reasoning level is NOT monotonic on writing quality.** `low` is worse than
BOTH its neighbours on honesty: it is the only cell in the row with a
fabrication, the only one that dropped a negative finding, and the only one
that returned an empty response. A two-point sweep that happened to sample
`off` and `low` would have concluded that thinking degrades honesty; a sweep
of `off` and `medium` would have concluded thinking is free of cost. Both
conclusions would have been wrong, and this is the argument for sweeping every
level rather than the endpoints.

**The owner's hypothesis is VINDICATED on this row, having been falsified on
the knowledge row.** He predicted `medium` as the cheapest level giving high
quality. On knowledge work the plateau starts at `low` and `medium` is
overspend; on writing, `medium` is the first level that is actually clean.
**The cheapest adequate level is task-dependent**, which is a stronger and
more useful result than either row alone, and it is why F69's scope is
deliberately confined to knowledge work.

**The cost is not small and is not hidden.** `medium` is **19x** `off`'s wall
time (4,277.6s against 225.2s) for +4 clean drafts, at a 498s median per item.
Nothing in this row is interactive: no level reaches a 30s median. Drafting on
this model is a batch activity at any setting that produces usable output.

**Still open:** the `xhigh` cell. If it also scores 6/7 with clean honesty
metrics, `medium` wins on cost alone; if it scores higher, the row's
recommendation moves and the cost question sharpens further.

## E44: what happens when the budget stops being the constraint? (2026-08-15, pre-registered before any run)

**Why this exists.** Owner instruction, after seeing that `run_matters.py`
would have killed the E43 long matters at 600s: *"I want to see what happens
when these tasks have huge token and time budgets available - what can they do
and how long do they really take?"* Proposed 90 min / 100k tokens and 180 min /
300k tokens on the toughest matters.

**Three measured facts reshaped the design before it was registered.**

1. **300,000 tokens is not reachable.** `n_ctx_train` for
   Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M is **262,144**, and the prompt shares that budget.
   Arm B is registered at **200,000**, which fits with room.
2. **The CLOCK binds before the token ceiling in both arms.** Sustained
   generation measured on this model today is **12.02 tok/s** (E42 writing
   `medium`: 51,367 completion tokens over 4,273.1s of item wall). 90 min =
   5,400s admits ~64,900 tokens; 180 min = 10,800s admits ~129,800. Neither
   arm can reach its token ceiling, and generation slows further as the KV
   grows. **This is registered as a known property, not discovered later:**
   the arms differ in TIME, and the token numbers are headroom rather than
   the binding constraint.
3. **Memory is not a risk, and this was checked against the deadlock rule.**
   Qwen3.8 is a DeltaNet hybrid: llama-server reports KV for only **16 of 64
   layers** (2,048 MiB at 32,768 cells = 64 KiB/token), the other 48 holding a
   constant 149.62 MiB recurrent state. So a full 262,144 context is
   16,384 MiB of KV; with the 15,088 MiB model that is **~31 GiB total**,
   against 112 GiB free and the ~60 GiB threshold in
   docs/memory-edge-deadlock.md. Arm B at `-c 262144` stays under it.

**What the evidence predicts, stated before the run.** Across **402 graded
items on 2026-08-15, `finish_reason: length` occurred exactly 5 times** - all
five in E33 coding, all at exactly 8,192 of 8,192. Every other item returned
`stop`. The largest completion ever observed on this box is **13,156 tokens**
(E42 writing `medium`), and on knowledge work the maximum is **967** (E42
`xhigh`). **The budget has never bound on knowledge work.** So the honest
prior is that arms A and B will produce near-identical answers and the
experiment will show that budget was never the constraint on matters - which
is itself the answer to the owner's question.

**Arms.** All local, Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M, b10435, `-np 1`, temperature 0,
`thinking=xhigh`. xhigh is chosen deliberately over E42's `low`
recommendation: it is the setting that SPENDS the most tokens, so it is the
setting most likely to use headroom. A budget probe run at the cheapest
setting would answer nothing.

| arm | items | max_tokens | request timeout | `-c` | KV |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | m11, m12, m13 | 100,000 | 16,967s (derived) | 131,072 | 8,192 MiB |
| B | m11, m12, m13 | 200,000 | 33,633s (derived) | 262,144 | 16,384 MiB |
| C | the 5 capped coding tasks | 100,000 | 16,967s (derived) | 131,072 | 8,192 MiB |

**The 90/180-minute budgets are HEADROOM, not kill switches, and this is a
deliberate departure from the instruction as literally worded.** The owner
asked for a 90-minute and a 180-minute time budget. Implementing those as
request timeouts was wired up and then removed before any run, because **an
HTTP request timeout returns NOTHING** - not the answer, not the token count,
not the wall time. Killing a generation at 90 minutes would destroy exactly
the measurement the experiment exists to take, on precisely the items most
likely to be long. That is the E33-void failure mode (a fixed timeout under a
raised budget), and re-creating it here on purpose would be worse than
inheriting it by accident.

So the CAP is `max_tokens`, which returns `finish_reason: length` together
with the tokens and the answer, and the request timeout sits above it at the
derived floor. **Duration is therefore MEASURED, not bounded** - "how long do
they really take" is answered by reading `seconds` off each record rather than
by a clock that stops it. If a matter runs past 90 minutes that is a result,
and the monitor surfaces it while it is happening.

Arm C is `parse_semver`, `normalize_path`, `roman_roundtrip`, `word_break`,
`eval_expr` - the only items in this repo that have ever hit a cap. The owner
chose to add them: the matters answer his question, and arm C tests the one
place a budget demonstrably bit.

**Baseline for A and B** is E43 at `max_tokens 24,576` (queue 7, already
registered). **Baseline for C** is E33's capped run and the E33 RE-RUN 2 at
24,576 (queued).

**Predictions. The FIELD is named in each. Bands are set high deliberately -
my registered bands have sat BELOW the measured result in E37, E38, the E42
knowledge row and the E42 writing row, four in a row in the same direction.**

1. **`finish_reason` is `stop` for all 3 matters in BOTH arms A and B.** No
   matter reaches even 100,000 tokens. If any returns `length`, the budget was
   a real constraint on legal work and E43's 24,576 is suspect.
2. **Arm A and arm B produce the SAME score** on all 3 matters, +/- 1 point of
   45 (3 x 15). If they differ by more, generation is not deterministic at
   these lengths and F59 does not extend to 100k-token generations - which
   would be a finding about the box, not the model.
3. **`completion_tokens` for the hardest matter (m11 or m13) is 2,000-25,000**
   in arm A. The registered band is wide because nothing on this corpus has
   been measured at any budget above 2,000.
4. **Total score across m11+m12+m13 in arm A is 18-38 of 45.** F60 measured
   m11 at 6/15 and m13 at 7/15 for OTHER models at `max_tokens 2000`; this is
   a different model with 50x the budget.
5. **Arm C: at least 3 of the 5 capped tasks return `stop` instead of
   `length`,** and at least 2 that previously scored 0 now pass. If all 5
   still hit `length` at 100,000 the model is looping, not thinking, and that
   is a much more interesting result than a score.
6. **Arm C's per-task wall exceeds 600s for at least one task.** These are the
   tasks that spent 8,192 tokens without finishing.

**Falsifier: if arm B differs from arm A on any matter, the whole
"budget was never the constraint" reading collapses** and E43's 24,576 has to
be re-examined before its results are used for the routing verdict.

**Cost, and the runaway guard.** With the caps on `max_tokens` rather than the
clock, the theoretical worst case is large: arm A 3 x 4.7h, arm B 3 x 9.3h,
arm C 5 x 4.7h. **That worst case requires the model to generate 100,000-200,000
tokens per item, which prediction 1 says it will not do** - the largest
completion ever observed on this box is 13,156 tokens, about 18 minutes. The
expected runtime is therefore ~20 min/item, and the theoretical ceiling exists
only because the cap was moved off the clock to preserve data.

The guard is observation, not a timeout: the queue log is monitored per item,
and any item still running well past 90 minutes will be visible while it
happens and can be killed by hand. A run killed that way loses one item's data
and is recorded as such; a run killed by a request timeout loses it silently,
which is the distinction the whole design turns on. Runs after queue 7.

### E42 RESULT - writing row complete, and the `xhigh` cell is NOT resolvable at this budget

| level | clean | `fabrication_rate` | `negative_retention` | completion tokens | max item | wall | median/item |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| off | 2/7 | 0.000 | 1.00 | 2,225 | 418 | 225.2s | 33.3s |
| low | 4/7 | 0.143 | 0.80 | 30,400 | 8,093 | 2,546.4s | 338.0s |
| **medium** | **6/7** | **0.000** | **1.00** | 51,367 | 13,156 | 4,277.6s | 498.2s |
| xhigh | 6/7* | 0.000 | 1.00 | 75,209 | **16,384 (capped)** | 6,285.1s | 1,000.4s |

**\* The two 6/7 scores are NOT the same result and must not be compared as
though they were.** `medium`'s single miss is a 201-word draft against a
120-200 band - one word, gradeable, a real near-miss. `xhigh`'s single miss is
`plain_english` hitting `max_tokens=16384` with `finish_reason: length`,
**52,490 characters of reasoning and an empty `output`**. It spent 1,377s -
23 minutes - on a 120-200 word plain-English rewrite and emitted no draft at
all.

**That is F20: a truncation is a HARNESS result, not a capability result.**
Scoring it as a miss would blame the model for our budget. So the honest
statement is that the `xhigh` cell is **6 of 6 gradeable items clean, with the
seventh unresolved**, and it cannot be ranked against `medium` until
`plain_english` is re-run with headroom. The harness already did the right
thing on the derived metrics - it reported `FABRICATION 0/6`, excluding the
ungradeable item from the denominator rather than counting it as honest.

**RECORDED AS AN OPEN GAP rather than rounded away.** E42's recommendation for
the writing row is `medium` on the evidence in hand, and that would not change
even if `xhigh` resolved to 7/7: `xhigh` costs **47% more wall** (6,285s
against 4,278s) and **46% more tokens** (75,209 against 51,367) for at most
one more clean draft, and E42's knowledge row already found `xhigh` bought
nothing there. But "would not change the recommendation" is not the same as
"resolved", and the re-run is queued rather than waived.

**Token spend rises monotonically with effort even where quality does not:**
2,225 -> 30,400 -> 51,367 -> 75,209, a **34x** spread from `off` to `xhigh`.
Reasoning characters go 0 -> 90,807 -> 140,766 -> 237,231. The quality peak is
at `medium`, one step before the token peak.

**The sixth cap hit, and the first outside coding.** Before this cell, every
`finish_reason: length` on this box was an E33 coding task at 8,192. This one
is a WRITING task at 16,384, which means the "budget has never bound outside
coding" prior recorded in E44's registration was true when written and is now
superseded. Declared as E44 AMENDMENT 1 below, before E44 runs.

### E44 AMENDMENT 1 (declared 2026-08-15 14:45, BEFORE any E44 arm runs)

**New evidence from the E42 writing `xhigh` cell weakens the prior this
experiment was registered on. The predictions are NOT rewritten to match it.**

E44's registration recorded that across 402 graded items, `finish_reason:
length` had occurred exactly 5 times, all E33 coding at 8,192, and that the
budget "has never bound on knowledge work". A sixth has now occurred and it is
**not** coding: `plain_english` at `thinking=xhigh` consumed the full
`max_tokens=16384` with 52,490 characters of reasoning and produced an **empty
output**, on a task asking for 120-200 words.

Three things follow, all declared before the arms run.

1. **Prediction 1 stands exactly as registered** - `finish_reason` is `stop`
   for all 3 matters in both arms. I now think it is **less likely to hold**
   than when I wrote it, and I am saying so rather than quietly revising the
   band. Pre-registration is worth nothing if a prediction gets improved every
   time adjacent evidence lands. If it fails, it fails on the record.
2. **The runaway case moved from theoretical to demonstrated, which matters
   because arms A and B run at `xhigh`.** The registration justified `xhigh`
   as "the setting most likely to use headroom"; that is now evidenced rather
   than assumed - at `xhigh` this model will spend an entire budget on a short
   task and emit nothing. At 100,000 tokens that is ~2.3 hours for one matter;
   at 200,000, ~4.6 hours. The worst case in the cost section is no longer
   implausible and the monitor is the guard that matters.
3. **An empty output at the cap is a REAL RESULT for E44, not a failed run.**
   If the toughest matters produce 100,000 tokens of reasoning and no answer,
   that is the finding - it says maximum effort on this model does not
   converge on hard legal work, which is far more useful than a score. The
   grading must therefore distinguish `truncated` from `wrong`, which
   `run_matters.py` supports by recording `finish_reason` and

**One control already exists:** E43 arm A runs the same three matters at
`thinking=low` and `max_tokens 24,576`. If `xhigh` runs away where `low`

**Superseded fact, corrected for the record:** the registration's "largest
completion ever observed on this box is 13,156 tokens" was true when written
(E42 writing `medium`) and is now 16,384 - but that value is a CAP, not a
natural stopping point, so the largest *voluntary* completion remains 13,156.
The distinction is the point of this amendment.

### E41 RESULT - n=0, the harness check (2026-08-15)

`--tier l3 --distractors 0`, `thinking=low`, `-c 32768`, `max_tokens 4096`,
b10435, kernel 7.0.0-28. Pack 13,221 chars - byte-identical in length to the
L2 pack, as designed.

**Prediction 1 HELD.** 12/12 `correct`, with a category split identical to
`e42-know-low` (the anchor set by AMENDMENT 1): date_effective 3/3,
revocation 2/2, precedence 2/2, multihop 3/3, exhaustive 1/1, underspecified
1/1. `outcome_counts` is `{'correct': 12}` - no `wrong_document`, which is
correct at n=0 where there are no distractors to be confused by.

**A near-miss worth recording, because the reflex it corrects is the expensive
one.** A per-item diff against `e42-know-low` showed P1 and P2 returning
different answer TEXT. Two config values also differed between the runs
(`-c` 32768 vs 16384, `max_tokens` 4096 vs 8192), so the obvious reading was
that context size perturbs generation at temperature 0 - which would have been
a significant caveat on F59 and on every cross-run comparison in this repo.

**That reading was wrong, and checking took one command.** L3 rescopes 11 of
its 12 questions so each names its agreement - "the Supplier" becomes
"Calderwood Advisory" - which E41's registration states explicitly as a design
requirement. **The prompts are different, so different text is the expected
result.** Only 1 of 12 questions is textually identical between the tiers.

The genuinely notable number is the other direction: 11 prompts changed and
only 2 answers changed, so 9 rescoped questions returned byte-identical text.

F59 is untouched. No claim about `-c` and determinism is made here, because
the comparison that appeared to support one was not like-for-like. The sweep
itself is internally clean: n=0, 4 and 9 all run at `-c 32768` with the same
questions, so the only variable across the sweep is pack size, which is what
E41 exists to vary.

### E41 RESULT - the falsifier FIRED. Scale to ~21K tokens is not a boundary either.

All arms: b10435, kernel 7.0.0-28, `-c 32768`, `-np 1`, temperature 0,
`max_tokens 4096`, full-offload gate passing. Qwen3.8 at `thinking=low` per
AMENDMENT 1; the workhorse has no equivalent setting.

| n | pack chars | prompt tokens | Qwen3.8 | wall | median | workhorse | wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 13,221 | 3,625 | **12/12** | 485.6s | 36.2s | 5/12 | 14.1s |
| 4 | 49,076 | 11,441 | **12/12** | 581.1s | 45.6s | - | - |
| 9 | 93,920 | 21,217 | **12/12** | 640.2s | 47.8s | 4/12 | 57.5s |

**The registered falsifier fired: `correct` at n=9 EQUALS `correct` at n=0.**
E41 said what that means - the boundary has not been found, rather than that
there isn't one. This is the **third instrument saturated in a day**, after
L1 (20/20) and L2 (12/12).

**Prediction 1 HELD.** n=0 is 12/12, reproducing the `e42-know-low` anchor.

**Predictions 2, 3 and 4 all FALSIFIED, in the same direction as every other
band I have registered today.**

- P2 registered n=9 at **7-11** and at least 2 below n=0. Measured **12**,
  above the band, with a drop of **zero**.
- P3 registered `wrong_document` >= 1 at n=9. Measured **0**. Nine
  structurally parallel agreements with deliberately confusable figures, and
  it never once reported a cap, retainer or retention period from the wrong
  contract.
- P4 registered `multihop` at **0-2 of 3** and lowest-scoring at n=9. Measured
  **3/3**, tied top. Every category held at 100%.

**Prediction 5 HELD - the control degrades more.** The workhorse drops 5 -> 4
across the same span while Qwen3.8 drops 0. The gap widens from 7 to 8 points.
Note the workhorse's failures are the SAME ones at both sizes -
`precedence` 0/2 and `multihop` 0/3 at n=0 and n=9 alike - so it is not
degrading under scale so much as failing at the reasoning regardless of it.
Its one lost point is `date_effective` 2/3 -> 1/3.

**Cost of 7x the context: 32% more wall** (485.6s -> 640.2s) and a median
moving 36.2s -> 47.8s. Retrieval over a folder of ten agreements is cheap on
this model; it is the reasoning that costs, and that cost is already paid at
n=0.


**CORRECTION TO E41 AMENDMENT 1: my overflow claim was WRONG, and the run
proves it.**

AMENDMENT 1 changed `max_tokens` 8192 -> 4096 and justified it by arguing that
n=9 at 8,192 would need 33,801 tokens against a 32,768 context - an overflow
of 1,033 on the one arm that matters. **The measured prompt is 21,217 tokens,
not the 25,609 I estimated.** So the original config would have been
21,217 + 8,192 = **29,409 of 32,768 - it FITS, with 3,359 spare.** There was
no overflow to catch.

The error is a ruler error of exactly the kind flagged one message earlier and
then repeated: I measured **3.67 chars/token on the L2 pack** and applied it
to a pack that is mostly distractor text, which tokenizes at **4.43
chars/token**. Distractors are boilerplate services-agreement prose and
compress better than the dense base documents. The estimate ran **20.6% high**,
and it ran high in the direction that manufactures an alarm.

| n | chars | tokens | chars/token |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 13,221 | 3,625 | 3.647 |
| 4 | 49,076 | 11,441 | 4.289 |
| 9 | 93,920 | 21,217 | 4.427 |

**What the amendment got right, and why it still stands:** the queue passed
8,192 where the registration said 4,096, and running the registered value is
correct on its own terms regardless of whether the wrong one would have fit.
Naming `thinking=low` was required by F65 and was genuinely missing. Both
changes were right; **one of the two stated reasons was not.** The sweep is
unaffected - every arm ran at one config - and no result changes.

Recorded because a justification that sounded rigorous and was arithmetically
wrong is worth more as a correction than as a quiet edit. The lesson is the
one already written into `development-discipline.md`: a ratio measured on one
corpus is not a ruler for a different corpus, and "measured" is not the same
as "measured on THIS text".

**`interval_map` is the informative one: timeout -> truncated -> pass.** At

failures resolving into a correct answer, and it is the clearest single piece

than padding.

already reported: this model handles well-specified self-contained problems
and struggles when the requirement is about efficiency rather than
correctness.

### E42 coding row, fourth cell: `xhigh` ABANDONED at 3 of 8, and why

**The cell was killed mid-run. This is a deviation from the registration and

|---|---|---|
| glob_match | pass, 13,836 tok, 1,148.9s | **truncated at 24,576**, 2,078.4s |
| round_decimal | pass, 6,279 tok, 517.8s | **truncated at 24,576**, 2,083.5s |
| kmerge | pass, 4,692 tok, 386.4s | **truncated at 24,576**, 2,082.9s |

`kmerge` is solved at `medium` in 4,692 tokens. At `xhigh` it spent five times

### OPERATOR ERROR: killing the runner orphaned its server and cost four runs

Killing the `xhigh` cell killed only the python runner. Its child
`llama-server` (pid 266692) survived, so when queue 6b advanced, the Rule 9
quiet-GPU guard refused the next four jobs:

```
FAIL: llama-server already running (pids: ['266692']).
      hint: a busy GPU voids the timing columns of this run
```

E40 workhorse, E40 Mistral-24B, **E39** and E33 RE-RUN 2 each exited rc=2 in
0s. **The guard worked exactly as designed** - it refused to produce four runs
whose timing columns would have been silently wrong, which is far better than
the alternative. The fault was entirely in the kill.

E39 is the comparison against the incumbent coding model on the same eight
expert tasks, so its loss would have left Qwen3.8's 7/8 without a baseline.
All four are re-queued: queue 10 carries E39 and the E33 re-run ahead of E44
because they are verdict-critical and short; queue 11 carries the two E40
writing arms at the tail. The orphan was reaped before E43 arm A started, and
that arm is running on its own fresh server, so nothing already collected is
contaminated.

**The lesson, for the runbook:** killing an eval runner requires reaping the
server it started. `pkill -x llama-server` after any manual kill, verified with
`pgrep -x`, before the next job is allowed to start.

`max_tokens 24576`, request timeout 4,396s derived, `-c 32768`, b10435,
temperature 0, all 13 matters, `thinking=low`.

**Headline: 59/65 (90.8%), zero traps reproduced anywhere in the run, and no
truncation - all 13 returned `stop`, the largest answer using 3,096 tokens of
the 24,576 budget (12.6%).**

| matter | score | | matter | score |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| m01-scope-variation | 4/5 | | m08-revenue-recognition | 5/5 |
| m02-fee-termination | 5/5 | | m09-capitalisation-split | **3/5** |
| m03-rate-increase | 4/5 | | m10-receivables-provision | 5/5 |
| m04-notice-pilon | 5/5 | | m11-limitation-clocks | **5/5** |
| m05-redundancy-formula | 5/5 | | m12-liability-cap-basis | **5/5** |
| m06-erasure-retention | 4/5 | | m13-interest-two-clocks | **5/5** |
| m07-breach-notification | 4/5 | | | |

**A SPECIFICATION ERROR IN MY OWN REGISTRATION, declared before resolving
anything.** E43's predictions were registered "out of 195 (15 points each)".
**That scale does not exist.** F60's `/15` column is the SUM ACROSS THREE
MODELS, each scored out of 5 - its own text says so ("m12 returned 4/5 from
all three models"). The real scale is 5 elements per matter, 65 for one arm. I
read an aggregate column as a per-model scale and built four bands on it.

This is the F65 failure again in a new place: a prediction that names a
quantity which cannot be measured as stated is not falsifiable. It is recorded
rather than silently rescaled.

- **Prediction 1 is UNRESOLVABLE as written.** For information only, and not
  as a resolution: its 90-150 of 195 band is 46-77%, which on the real scale
  is about 30-50 of 65. The measured 59 sits above it. That would be the sixth
  consecutive band below the result, but a band on a non-existent scale should
  not be credited as a miss OR a hit.
- **Prediction 4 is FALSIFIED, and this is the substantive finding.** It
  registered that m11, m12 and m13 would be the three LOWEST-scoring matters,
  on F60's theory that a period which must be walked is what discriminates.
  They are the three **highest**, at 5/5 each. m11 is described in F60 as the
  second-hardest matter in the whole corpus; this model scores full marks on
  it. **F60's theory of what makes a matter hard does not transfer to this
  model.** The matters built specifically to defeat the previous generation
  are the ones it finds easiest.
- **Prediction 5 HELD.** Zero `length` finishes at 24,576. The budget was
  never within 4x of binding.
- **Predictions 2 and 3 are PENDING** - the incumbent arms and the `xhigh` arm
  have not run.

**The saturation falsifier missed by ONE ELEMENT.** It registered "above 180
of 195", which is 92.3%, or 60 of 65 on the real scale. Measured: 59. So this
corpus is NOT declared saturated, by a single point, and it is the first
instrument all day to leave any headroom at all.

**Where the six lost points are:** m09-capitalisation-split loses two
(elements 4 and 5), and m01, m03, m06 and m07 lose one each. m07 is the matter
F60 calls the hardest in the corpus, and it scored 4/5. The failures are
spread thinly rather than concentrated, which is the profile of a model near
the top of an instrument rather than one defeated by a particular mechanism.

**Zero traps is the number worth carrying to a client.** The corpus embeds
specific wrong answers - a service credit computed on the wrong month's rate,
a limitation clock run from the letter rather than the notification, a
deadline extended over a weekend that the rules say is not extended. It
reproduced none of them.

**Bearing on E44.** The three matters E44 arm A and B were built around are
m11, m12 and m13 precisely because F60 called them the hardest. This model
scores 5/5 on all three at `low`, using 2,678, 1,567 and 3,096 tokens. E44
therefore no longer measures "can it answer the toughest matters given room" -
it already can, cheaply. What E44 now measures is whether `xhigh` RUNS AWAY on
problems `low` solves in under 3,100 tokens. Given the coding row truncated
3 of 3 at `xhigh` on tasks `medium` solved in 4,700, that is a live question
and arguably a more useful one. The arms are left exactly as registered.

## E45: does Qwen3.8 fix the ONE place the routing guide says the workhorse is unsafe? (2026-08-15, pre-registered before any run)

**Why this exists.** Owner instruction: keep testing other concepts, find its
strength. Every instrument so far has probed the same shape - closed-record
reading and reasoning - and three of them saturated. This probes a different
capability with a **named, measured, reproducible incumbent failure** to aim at.

`reports/2026-07-16-local-model-routing-guide.md` says:

> A tool call whose behaviour depends on a condition -> **Mistral-Small-24B**.
> The Qwen family and gpt-oss apply conditional flags *unconditionally* - 0/5
> on the not-urgent branch. Mistral scored 100% (E33). **This is the one place
> the workhorse is unsafe.**

Qwen3.8 is a Qwen model, so the family prior says it fails. But the defect is
**reasoning inside the tool call**, and reasoning is precisely what this
generation added. If it fixes 0/5, the guide loses its only carve-out and the
model earns a capability the current workhorse does not have. That is a
strength worth looking for, and a clean falsifiable question either way.

**Instrument.** `tools/tooluse_harness_v2.py`, the E33 benchmark, restricted to
its `conditional` category:

| task | what it tests |
|---|---|
| `c1-urgent` | balance EUR 7,400, rule says >5,000 gets URGENT -> URGENT **must** appear |
| `c2-not-urgent` | balance EUR 300, same rule -> URGENT must **not** appear. **This is the 0/5.** |
| `c3-vat` | compute VAT at 23% and a total, put them in the spreadsheet |

`c1` and `c3` are the controls. A model that never writes URGENT passes `c2`
and fails `c1`, so `c2` alone proves nothing.

**Two harness defects fixed before any arm ran, both the same class already hit
four times today.**

1. **`max_tokens` was hard-coded to 1,200.** That is the E33-era value and it
   cannot hold a reasoning trace - Qwen3.8 spends thousands of tokens before
   answering, so a reasoning arm left at 1,200 measures the cap, not the model
   (F20). Now a flag, and **every E45 arm runs at 4,096** including the
   incumbents, so the comparison is internally like-for-like rather than
   inheriting E33's number.
2. **The request timeout was hard-coded to 180s**, which a reasoning model
   blows through. Now derived from `max_tokens`.

**Held FIXED deliberately: `temperature 0.2` and `runs=5`.** Every E33 number
this is measured against used them. They are not oversights and must not be
"improved" to temperature 0 - that would break the like-for-like comparison
the benchmark exists for. Tool use is therefore NOT deterministic here and the
headline is a success RATE over five runs.

**Arms.** All local, b10435, `--jinja`, `-c 32768`, `-np 1`, `max_tokens 4096`,
`runs 5`.

| arm | model | thinking |
|---|---|---|
| A | Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M | `off` |
| B | Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M | `low` |
| C | Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M | `medium` |
| D | Qwen3-30B-A3B-2507 (incumbent workhorse) | n/a |
| E | Mistral-Small-3.1-24B (the 100% reference) | n/a |

D and E are RE-RUN rather than cited from E33: different build (F63), different
date, and now a different token budget.

**Predictions. The FIELD is `success_rate` on the named task, over 5 runs.
Bands are set HIGH on purpose - mine have sat at or below the measured result
five or six times today, and continuing to register low bands would be
repeating a known error rather than learning from it.**

1. **`c2-not-urgent` for the workhorse (arm D): 0.0-0.4.** A reproduction
   check of E33's 0/5. If it now passes, E33's finding has decayed and the
   routing guide's carve-out needs revisiting on its own.
2. **`c2-not-urgent` for Qwen3.8 at `off` (arm A): 0.0-0.6.** With reasoning
   disabled it should behave like the family prior.
3. **`c2-not-urgent` for Qwen3.8 at `low` OR `medium` reaches >= 0.8.** This
   is the discriminating claim and the reason the experiment exists.
4. **Parse rate is 1.0 for every Qwen3.8 arm** - structured `tool_calls`, no
   native format leaked as text. F38 recorded leakage as the Coder's failure,
   not the workhorse's, and Qwen3.8 is not the Coder.
5. **`c1-urgent` and `c3-vat` are >= 0.8 for Qwen3.8 at EVERY level including
   `off`.** These need no conditional reasoning, so if they fail at `off` the
   task is measuring something other than what it claims.

**Falsifier: if `c2-not-urgent` is <= 0.4 for Qwen3.8 at every level, the
conditional-flag defect is architectural to the Qwen family and survived a
generation change.** The routing guide's Mistral carve-out then stands
unchanged and is strengthened by a second generation of evidence, which is a
useful result rather than a null one.

### E43 RESULT - arm B (`xhigh`): 60/65. Maximum effort buys ONE element for 2.5x the tokens.

| | arm A `low` | arm B `xhigh` |
|---|---|---|
| total | 59/65 | **60/65** |
| answer tokens | 23,980 | **59,925** |
| largest single answer | 3,096 | 10,723 (44% of budget) |
| truncations | 0 | 0 |
| traps reproduced | **0** | **0** |

**The entire gain is m01-scope-variation, 4/5 -> 5/5.** Every other matter is
identical, including all four of arm A's other misses: m03 4/5, m06 4/5,
m07 4/5, m09 3/5. Maximum effort did not touch a single one of them.

**One element for 35,945 extra tokens.** That is the clearest cost-of-effort
number in the programme.

**Prediction 3 HELD.** It registered `low` and `xhigh` within 10 points of 195,
which rescales to about 3.3 of 65. The measured difference is **1**.

**Prediction 5 HELD for both arms.** Zero `length` finishes at 24,576; the
largest answer used 44% of the budget.

**The saturation falsifier did NOT fire, by nothing at all.** It registered
"above 180 of 195" - which is 0.9231, or **above 60.00 of 65**. Arm B scored
**exactly 60**. Equal, not above. Arm A missed the same line by one element at
59. Two arms, and the corpus is not declared saturated by a margin of zero.
This is stated rather than rounded either way: a falsifier that lands exactly
on its threshold is a fact about the registration, and the honest reading is
that this corpus is at the edge of saturation rather than clearly inside or
outside it.

**Zero traps at BOTH effort levels.** Across 26 matter-answers the corpus's
embedded wrong answers were reproduced not once.

**The runaway question, answered - and it is TASK-DEPENDENT.** E44 was
reframed on the theory that `xhigh` might run away on problems `low` solves
cheaply, because the coding row truncated 3 of 3 at this same 24,576 budget on
tasks `medium` solved in 4,700 tokens. On legal matters it does not run away:
13 of 13 converged, and the per-matter multiplier is not flat - 1.2x on
m05-redundancy-formula, 4.5x on m01-scope-variation. It spends most where
there is most to reason about.

**So runaway is a property of the TASK, not of the setting.** That is worth
more than either row alone, and it sharpens E44: the matters arms will likely
confirm the budget was never the constraint, while arm C - the coding tasks -
is where the headroom actually gets used. The arms stay as registered.

**Bearing on the routing verdict.** `low` is the setting for legal work: 59/65
against 60/65 for 40% of the tokens. The one extra element does not justify
2.5x the cost, and nothing in arm B's answers repaired the four misses that
matter.

| Qwen3.8 `xhigh` | 60/65 | 59,925 | 4,976s | **0** |

| Mistral-Small-24B | 45/65 | 8,129 | 581s | 1 |

**Prediction 2 HELD: Qwen3.8 beats every incumbent's total.** 59 > 53 > 45.
This is the discriminating claim the experiment existed for, and it holds.

**But the margin is the smallest of the programme, and this must not be
reported as another blowout.** On L2 it was 12/12 against 5/12. Here it is
90.8% against **81.5%** - six elements of 65. On the one instrument built by
someone who was not trying to make this model look good, the gap narrows to a
quarter of what the purpose-built tiers showed.

**Qwen3.8 LOSES three matters to the workhorse**, and that is stated first
rather than buried under the total:

| matter | Qwen3.8 `low` | workhorse |
|---|---|---|
| m09-capitalisation-split | **3/5** | **5/5** |
| m01-scope-variation | 4/5 | 5/5 |
