cleanest possible baseline for a drop test, but it is not a difficulty probe and
must not be reported as one.

### Predictions (registered before any arm runs). The FIELD is named in each.

Bands are set high; this programme's have sat below the measured result eleven
times now.

1. **PRIMARY: for Qwen3.8-27B, `deep_correct` is at most 1 below
   `shallow_correct`** out of 10. If holding the question out costs the strong
   model nothing, E56's byte-identical result was retention and not a copy.
2. **CONTROL: `shallow_correct` for Qwen3.8-27B is 9 or 10 of 10**, matching its
   E54b standalone 10/10 to within one. If the shallow arm does not reproduce
   standalone, the scope preamble or the conversation framing changed the
   questions and the crossover's baseline is not a baseline.
3. **`wrong_document` is 0 on every arm and in both orders.** F74 measured zero
   wrong-document retrieval at 236,122 tokens and F82 measured zero across all
   three arms. Registered at zero deliberately: the most interesting available
   outcome is that removing the model's own prior answer is what makes
   wrong-document retrieval appear, and a band tolerating one would hide it.
4. **`recent` is 3/3 on every arm in both orders.** E56 measured 5/5 on all
   three. If a model misses a question about an agreement delivered moments
   earlier, it is not decaying with depth and the tier's framing is wrong.
5. **The workhorse's `deep_correct` is within 2 of its `shallow_correct`**, in
   either direction. Its L4 cells are the noisy ones - 5/10 standalone with
   three distinct failure shapes - so a wider band is honest rather than
   generous.
6. **B1 is not `correct` for the 8B or the workhorse in EITHER position.** Both
   scored `off_by_calendar` on it standalone: 72 hours from Friday afternoon
   lands on Easter Monday, and rule C.3 says the clock does not stop. A pass here
   would mean the conversation helped, which nothing predicts.
7. **`format_error` <= 2 per run**, no arm aborts on the per-turn context
   preflight, and every run records its real final history rather than the
   projection above.
8. **Byte-identical answers shallow-versus-deep will be MUCH rarer than E56's
   15/15**, because these are two separate runs rather than two turns of one.
   Registered so that a low number is read as the design working, not as
   instability.

**Falsifier: if Qwen3.8-27B's `deep_correct` is 3 or more below its
`shallow_correct`**, then E56's byte-identical headline WAS the own-answer
confound. F82 would need withdrawing to the much weaker claim that a model can
re-read its own answer at depth, and the routing guide's "load once, interrogate"
advice would need a stated turn limit for conversational use.

**Second falsifier, on the instrument rather than the models: if every arm
degrades on the same one or two questions and no others**, suspect those
questions before concluding anything about depth - the E54b lesson, applied to
this tier's own headline.

**Third falsifier, on the crossover itself: if a model's set-A and set-B shallow
scores differ by 2 or more** in a way E54b's standalone split does not predict,
the two sets are not interchangeable and the crossover is measuring set
difficulty rather than depth.

**Cost.** 6 runs x 18 turns, all local, no cloud spend. Estimated one to two
hours. No model here is near the >~60GiB memory edge, so the deadlock rules do
not bind.

## E58: can Qwen3.8 serve a TINY query quickly enough to be resident? (2026-08-19, pre-registered before any run)

**The question, sharpened by the owner:** not "which model is better" but *"can
3.8 serve tiny queries relatively quickly?"* If it can, one model serves
everything and the relay needs no routing. If it cannot, the workhorse stays
resident and document work is routed to the 27B by name.

**The traffic is now measured, not assumed.** `tools/relay_traffic_mix.py` over
the relay's own log - **952 requests, 2026-07-19 to 2026-08-14, 15 active days,
100% served by the workhorse**:

| prompt tokens | n | share of COUNT | median ms | share of TIME |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| under 1,000 | 869 | **91.3%** | 855 | 27.1% |
| 1,000-4,000 | 33 | 3.5% | 4,204 | 5.1% |
| 4,000-16,000 | 37 | 3.9% | 24,890 | 33.6% |
| 16,000-64,000 | 13 | 1.4% | 72,357 | 34.3% |

Median prompt **68 tokens**, p90 759, max 60,012. The 50 requests at or above
4,000 tokens are **5.3% of count and 67.9% of generation time**.

`tools/latency_matrix.py`, four arms (workhorse; 27B at `off`; 27B at `low`;
8B), three tiers drawn from that distribution rather than from taste, reps
weighted to the tier that decides it (chat 7, document 3, folder 2). Time to a
COMPLETE answer, not time for N tokens - capping generation would flatter a
model whose entire cost is that it thinks. Cold and warm reported separately so
the 45:1 prefill effect (F74) is not averaged into a single misleading number.
One serving config across all arms, `-b 512 -ub 128`, which E49 measured as the
27B's optimum and inert for `-b` - so it biases TOWARD the 27B and understates
the workhorse.

### Predictions (registered before any arm runs)

1. **PRIMARY: the 27B at `off` answers the chat tier in under 5s warm-median.**
   Under 5s is my threshold for "relatively quickly" in the owner's sense - a
   pause, not a wait.
2. **The workhorse's chat warm-median is within 2x of the relay's production
   855ms.** This is the calibration check: if the bench cannot reproduce the
   number the live service actually delivered, the bench is measuring something
   else and no comparison built on it is safe.
3. **The workhorse is 3-8x faster than the 27B at `off` on the chat tier.** The
   workhorse is MoE with roughly 3B active parameters against 27B dense, so
   the gap should be large and mostly per-token rather than prefill.
4. **`off` versus `low` on the chat tier is a bigger gap than workhorse versus
   27B-`off`.** F69 says the 27B has no middle setting; if that holds on tiny
   prompts too, the reasoning switch dominates the model choice.
5. **The 8B at `off`-equivalent beats the 27B at `off`** on the chat tier, being
   a third of the size.
6. **On the folder tier the 27B's cold time is dominated by prefill**, so its
   warm-median is at least 5x below its cold time.

**Falsifier: if the 27B at `off` lands under 2s warm-median on the chat tier**,
the two-model recommendation is wrong - it can serve the 91.3% acceptably and
should simply be made resident, since it wins every accuracy instrument and is
1.62 GiB smaller.

## E57 RESULTS (2026-08-19): the 27B does not decay at depth, the 8B does, and E56 could not tell those apart

Six runs, three models, two orders each. Every arm completed; `format_error` was
**0 everywhere** and `wrong_document` **0 everywhere**. Depth landed at
**69.3-72.5% of `-c 32768`**, against E56's 71-76% - the same depth, which is
what makes the two readable side by side.

| | standalone (E54b) | **shallow** | **deep** | degraded | `recent` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.8-27B `low` | 10/10 | **10/10** | **10/10** | **none** | 6/6 |
| Qwen3-8B | 9/10 | 9/10 | **6/10** | **4** | 6/6 |
| workhorse 30B-A3B | 5/10 | 3/10 | **5/10** | none | 6/6 |

**F83. Held out from its own answer, the 27B does not decay and the 8B does.**
E56 reported that no arm degraded at depth. For the 27B that survives contact
with the held-out design untouched. For the 8B it does not: it holds 5 of 5
paired anchors in E56 and loses **4 of 10** held-out questions here. The
difference between those two results is precisely the confound E57 was built to
remove, and it changed the result rather than qualifying it.

### What the 27B did, and the part that was not predicted

Ten of ten shallow, ten of ten deep, and its shallow arm reproduced its E54b
standalone score **exactly**, which was the registered control. Prediction 8
said byte-identical answers would be much rarer than E56's 15/15 because these
are two separate runs rather than two turns of one. **All ten of its answers are
byte-identical between the `ab` and `ba` runs** - same string, asked at turn 3
in one run and turn 16 in the other, twenty thousand tokens apart, across two
separate server processes. That is a determinism result E56 could not have
produced and E57 did not set out to measure.

### What the 8B did, and it is one failure mode rather than four

Four degradations, and the mechanism is visible in the token counts rather than
inferred: **the model reasons MORE at depth and lands worse.**

| | shallow | deep |
|---|---|---|
| `F1` | **correct** in 558 generated tokens | **truncated** at the 5,120 ceiling - 9.2x the reasoning, no answer |
| `P2` | **correct** in 1,376 tokens (`30 April 2026`) | **wrong** in 2,303 tokens (`31 March 2026`) |
| `X1` | **correct** in 539 tokens (`NO`) | **wrong** in 562 tokens (`YES`) |

`F1`'s deep cell is a BUDGET exhaustion, not a wrong answer - `finish_reason`
`length`, 13,891 characters of reasoning against 1,500 shallow. E55 already
warned that a small model used conversationally needs a bigger answer budget or
its failures read as capability, and this is that warning landing again on a
tier that raised the budget to 5,120 and still hit it. Counted honestly the 8B
is **3 genuine degradations and 1 truncation**, not 4 capability failures.

### The workhorse improved, and the tier cannot say much about it

3/10 shallow to 5/10 deep, with `P3` and `F1` both moving from wrong to correct.
Do not read that as depth helping. Its shallow arm is **below its own standalone
5/10**, so the shallow cell is near this instrument's floor and a floor cannot
degrade. What the tier does establish for the workhorse is negative and useful:
it never retrieved from the wrong document, and it answered every `recent` probe.

**One observation worth recording without over-reading it.** The workhorse scores
`X1` and `X2` **correct standalone and wrong in BOTH conversational positions** -
the two `defect_absent` traps, where the right answer is that nothing is
breached. The 8B gets both right shallow and both wrong deep. F76 says single
cells are noisy, and this is four cells across two models, so it is a lead
rather than a finding: the conversational framing may prime a model that has
just been asked what is wrong with a contract to keep finding things wrong.

### A grader defect, found by an arm rather than by the validator

`grade_multiturn` labelled a wrong `YES` as `over_revised` on **any** yes/no
item. That is correct for E56, whose only yes/no turn WAS the over-revision
probe, and wrong for E57, which contains no revisions at all - so `X1` and `X2`
were reported as over-revisions in a tier with nothing to over-revise.
`grade_answer_l4` calls the same answer `wrong`, so a yes/no item was scoring a
different label inside a conversation than outside one. **That is exactly the
divergence the `choice` branch was copied byte-for-byte to prevent, and `yes_no`
was missed.**

The repair gates `over_revised` on the turn actually being an over-revision
probe. It was NOT applied mid-queue - that would have graded later arms with
different code than earlier ones. Instead `tools/regrade_multiturn.py`
re-derived the labels from the stored answers, which is E54b's pattern and costs
no GPU:

- **Proven no-op first:** the tool reproduced the runner's own grading on arm 1
  with 0 cells moved, before any change. So every cell it moved afterwards is
  attributable to the repair alone.
- **Proven no-op on the prior tiers:** all six E55 and E56 runs regrade with
  **0 cells moved**, reproducing their published scores exactly.
- **On E57: 6 cells moved, all `over_revised` -> `wrong`, all `X1`/`X2`, and no
  `correct` count changed on any arm.**

The validator now carries a `says_yes_anyway` respondent that answers YES to a
want-NO item and asserts it grades `wrong` with `over_revised` at 0. **116/116.**
Nothing caught this before an arm produced it, because no synthetic respondent
had ever answered YES to a want-NO item - the signature table tested the shapes
I had thought of.

### Predictions: six held, two falsified, and both falsifications are the models beating the band

1. **PRIMARY - 27B `deep_correct` at most 1 below shallow. HELD**, at 0 below.
2. **CONTROL - 27B shallow 9 or 10. HELD** at 10/10, matching standalone exactly.
3. **`wrong_document` 0 on every arm and both orders. HELD.** Removing the
   model's own prior answer did NOT make wrong-document retrieval appear.
4. **`recent` 3/3 every arm, both orders. HELD**, 6/6 on all three models.
5. **Workhorse deep within 2 of shallow. HELD**, at exactly +2 - the edge of the
   band, and in the improving direction.
6. **B1 not correct for the 8B or workhorse in either position. FALSIFIED for the
   8B**, which answered `6 April 2026 at 14:30` in BOTH positions - walking 72
   hours through the Easter Monday holiday that rule C.3 says does not stop the
   clock, where standalone it scored `off_by_calendar`. Held for the workhorse.
7. **`format_error` <= 2 per run. HELD** at 0 on all six; one `truncated`, which
   is a different outcome and is reported as one.
8. **Byte-identical shallow-vs-deep much rarer than E56's 15/15. FALSIFIED for
   the 27B** at 10/10 across two separate runs. Held for the 8B and workhorse,
   both 5/10.

**Twelve and thirteen.** That is the twelfth and thirteenth time this
programme's registered bands have sat below the measured result, and no
registered falsifier has ever fired.

### What this does to F82, and what it does not

**The primary falsifier did not fire, so F82's headline stands for the 27B.**
Its byte-identical deep answers in E56 were retention, not a copy - it
reproduces the same answers when its own answer is removed, and reproduces them
across separate processes.

**F82's "no arm degraded" is AMENDED for the 8B.** E56 could not distinguish
holding from re-reading, and for the small model the distinction turns out to
matter: 5 of 5 anchors held when its own answer was available, 6 of 10 when it
was not. Anyone quoting E56's result for a small model must now quote E57's
instead.

**What E57 still cannot separate:** depth from distraction. At turn 14 the model
has a longer history AND ten more documents, exactly as in E56. A third arm
padded with non-document material would separate them and has not been run.
Nor does this tier speak to spontaneous retrieval - every question carries a
preamble pointing at the pack, which is the realistic advisory case and is not
the same as the model finding the pack unprompted.

## E59: is MTP speculative decoding OUTPUT-PRESERVING on this model? (2026-08-19, pre-registered before any run)

**Why now.** Qwen3.8-27B was trained with multi-step Multi-Token Prediction, and
this box has been loading those weights and discarding them. From the E57 27B
serverlog, unprompted:

```
W model has unused tensor blk.64.nextn.eh_proj.weight (size = 29491200 bytes) -- ignoring
W model has unused tensor blk.64.nextn.enorm.weight  (size = 20480 bytes) -- ignoring
```

`/opt/models/staging/Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf` retains the `blk.64.nextn.*` MTP
layers, and llama.cpp build 770 (`9e40df63b`) supports `--spec-type` with
`draft-mtp` among its values. **No run in this repo has ever passed it**, so
every published Qwen3.8 figure was measured with a draft head resident and idle.

**And a named reason to distrust it.** A current llama.cpp Qwen3.8 investigation
reports strong MTP throughput *alongside deterministic-output divergence still
under investigation*. Speculative decoding is supposed to be mathematically
exact - the draft is verified against the target, so accepted tokens are the
tokens the target would have produced. If output moves, either the
implementation is not exact on this model or the acceptance path is wrong. That
is a correctness question, and a score cannot answer it: two runs can both be
13/13 while disagreeing on every word.

### The probe is E57's determinism result, which is why this is worth running now

E57's 27B produced **ten of ten byte-identical answers across two separate runs
and two separate server processes**, asked at turn 3 in one order and turn 16 in
the other. That is a measured noise floor of **zero**, and it makes this model an
unusually sensitive detector: re-run the identical conversation with one flag
changed and any divergence is attributable to the flag.

**Design: one variable.** E57's 27B arms ran `server_extra=''`. The MTP arms run
`server_extra='--spec-type draft-mtp'` and nothing else - same model, same
`-c 32768`, same `-np 1`, same `max_tokens 5120`, same `reasoning_effort: low`,
same conversation scripts, same grader. `tools/diff_run_answers.py` refuses the
comparison unless model, conversation, ctx, max_tokens and thinking all match
and only `server_extra` differs.

Both orders are run, so the comparison is **26 graded cells**, and it re-tests
E57's cross-run byte-identity property under the new config as well as against
the old one.

### Predictions (registered before any arm runs)

1. **PRIMARY: all 26 answer strings are byte-identical to their non-MTP
   counterparts.** This is what "speculative decoding is exact" means. It is
   registered as the expected result rather than the hoped-for one, because the
   alternative is a correctness defect and should be loud.
2. **`correct` is 13/13 on both MTP arms**, matching E57 exactly.
3. **Wall time improves by at least 1.2x on both arms.** MTP with a resident
   draft head should win something on a decode-heavy workload; below 1.2x it is
   not worth a serving-config change and the acceptance rate is the thing to
   look at next.
4. **The `unused tensor ... ignoring` warnings disappear from the serverlog.**
   This is the mechanical check that the flag did anything at all - without it a
   "no change" result could simply mean MTP never engaged, which would look
   identical to "MTP is exact" on every other measure.
5. **The `recent` probes stay 3/3 on both arms.**

**Falsifier: if ANY answer string differs**, MTP is not output-preserving on this
model at this build, the throughput number is irrelevant, and `--spec-type
draft-mtp` must not go near `serving.conf`. Report the divergence, not the speed.

**Second falsifier, on the instrument: if the `unused tensor` warnings persist**,
the flag did not engage and this experiment measured nothing - a null result here
would be an artefact, not a finding.

**Cost.** 2 runs x 18 turns on the 27B, local, no cloud spend. E57's arms took
695.9s and 565.3s, so roughly 20 minutes plus whatever MTP changes.

### E59 AMENDMENT 1 (2026-08-19, declared BEFORE any E59 arm ran)

New evidence arrived between pre-registration and the first run, so it is
declared here rather than used to explain a result afterwards.

**Two upstream llama.cpp issues, both bearing directly on prediction 1:**

- **#25618** - draft-model speculative decoding, `draft-mtp` and `draft-dspark`
  included, **changes greedy output on QUANTIZED target models**, reproduced on
  **Strix Halo with Vulkan**. Our target is `Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M` and our backend
  is Vulkan/RADV on gfx1151. That is our exact configuration.
- **#27151** - a Qwen3.8 report of MTP draft acceptance collapsing to **1 of 633**.

**Prediction 1 was registered as "all 26 answer strings byte-identical", on the
principle that speculative decoding is mathematically exact. The evidence above
says that principle does not hold in this implementation on quantized targets.
I now expect prediction 1 to be FALSIFIED**, and I am saying so before the run
rather than claiming afterwards that I knew. The prediction stands as
registered; what changes is my stated expectation of it, and the falsifier
becomes the likely outcome rather than the alarm.

**This makes the run MORE worth doing, not less.** If divergence is real on our
config, we will have measured it on an instrument with a zero noise floor, which
almost nobody has. If it is absent, that is a genuine surprise worth reporting.

**A third possibility the acceptance bug forces us to name:** MTP engages,
accepts almost nothing, output is byte-identical, and wall time is unchanged or
worse. That would satisfy predictions 1 and 2 while meaning nothing at all -
so **MTP acceptance must be recorded, not inferred from the wall time.**
Prediction 4 (the `unused tensor` warnings disappearing) proves the flag
engaged; it does not prove the draft was ever accepted.

### E59 DESIGN REVISION (same amendment): two settings, chat tier separated

The owner's framing sharpens the question from "is MTP exact" to **"can
Qwen3.8-27B + Vulkan + MTP make the 91.3% chat tier fast enough that routing
becomes unnecessary?"** Same-hardware reports put MTP at roughly **12.5 -> 24.1
tok/s** on Q4 under Vulkan on an EVO-X2, which is large enough to move E58's
2-second falsifier. So the design splits:

**Stage 1 - the correctness gate, and it is a GATE.** E57's `heldout-ab`
conversation re-run at `--spec-draft-n-max` **2** and **4**, each diffed against
the vanilla `ab` run cell by cell. 13 graded cells per setting.

> **MTP graduates only if the 27B stays 13/13 AND every answer string is
> unchanged.** The 27B is interesting *because* it is extraordinarily reliable
> in these instruments. Trading that away to make it resemble the workhorse
> defeats the purpose of serving it at all.

If a setting passes, its mirror `heldout-ba` run confirms the cross-run
byte-identity property. If MTP-2 passes and MTP-4 does not, MTP-2 is the
operating point. If neither passes, `--spec-type draft-mtp` does not go near
`serving.conf` and the two-model architecture stands.

**Stage 2 - chat-tier latency only**, and only for settings that passed stage 1.
Three arms (none / MTP-2 / MTP-4) on the chat prompts alone, capturing **warm
median, p95, generated tokens and MTP acceptance**. Not another 48-request
instrument: E57 supplies the quality probe and the traffic log already named the
tier that decides it.

**Deliberately postponed:** `n=6`, `n=12`, stacked n-gram speculation, quant
sweeps and any HIP build. Upstream MTP correctness and acceptance are actively
buggy, so the question is whether n=2 or n=4 *already* changes the architectural
decision. **HIP specifically is dropped rather than deferred** - same-hardware
evidence suggests Vulkan can be the better speculative-decoding backend on
Strix Halo even where ROCm wins elsewhere, so "we are on Vulkan" is recorded as
a fact about our figures, not treated as a defect to fix.

### E59 machine facts, recorded before the runs (Rule 8)

Captured 2026-08-19 from the live box, not from memory. Every E59 arm and the
E57 baseline it is compared against share all of these.

| fact | value |
|---|---|
| target model | `/opt/models/staging/Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf`, 866 tensors, GGUF v3, MTP layers present |
| llama.cpp | build 770, commit `9e40df63b` (worktree `b10435`) |
| backend | **Vulkan**, `RADV GFX1151`, driver `radv`, **Mesa 25.2.8-0ubuntu0.24.04.2**, Vulkan API 1.4.318 |
| kernel | `7.0.0-28-generic`; Livepatch client v10.16.2 active |
| **power profile** | **`balanced`** |
| context / slots | `-c 32768`, `-np 1`, `kv_unified = false` |
| flash attention | `flash_attn = auto` (never explicitly set, never swept) |
| batch flags | E57 baseline and E59 arms: **none**. (The E58 latency matrix uses `-b 512 -ub 128`; the two are not comparable on speed) |
| device memory | Vulkan0 reports 116,736 MiB, 110,917 free; the 27B occupies 17,452 MiB |

**`powerprofilesctl get` returns `balanced`, not `performance`.** Every figure
this repo has published for any model was measured on the balanced profile and
none of them says so. That is the thermal-state confound in its plainest form.
**E59 keeps `balanced`** so that it differs from its E57 baseline by the MTP flag
alone - switching the profile here would change two things at once and make a
divergence unattributable. A power-profile sweep is a separate experiment and is
now queued rather than folded in.

Mesa at 25.2.8 matches F57's record that Mesa has not drifted, so the graphics
stack is where that finding left it.

## E59 STAGE 1 RESULT (2026-08-19): MTP passes the correctness gate, and spends the determinism property to do it

| arm | correct | answer strings identical | **strict** identical | wall | decode |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| vanilla | 13/13 | - | - | 695.9s | 10.87 tok/s |
| MTP n=2 | 13/13 | **13/13** | 5/13 | 407.6s (1.71x) | 19.21 (**1.77x**) |
| **MTP n=4** | 13/13 | **13/13** | **10/13** | 376.9s (1.85x) | 22.65 (**2.08x**) |

**n=4 is better on every axis at once** - faster AND more deterministic - so n=2
is dropped from stage 2. Acceptance falls from 93.2% to 83.4%, but accepted
drafts per verification rise 1.86 -> 3.34 (effective 2.86 -> 4.34 tokens per
verification), and the extra accepted span more than pays for the lower rate.
Draft length was **not clamped**: n=4 genuinely offered 4-token drafts from a
model with `nextn_predict_layers = 1`, because llama.cpp's MTP drafter feeds the
single NextN mechanism forward until `n_max`.

**Prediction 1 HELD and AMENDMENT 1's expectation was WRONG.** The amendment,
written before the run on the strength of upstream #25618, said I expected all-
identical answers to be falsified. All 13 answer strings are identical on both
arms. #27151's acceptance collapse also did not reproduce - 83-93% here, in line
with #26750's ~91-92% on RADV/Vulkan.

**But #25618 is real, and it lands where a score cannot see it.** The full
completions moved on **8 of 13** cells at n=2 and **3 of 13** at n=4. The sharp
one is `F1`: **2,201 -> 1,289 generated tokens at n=2**, same final answer. That
is a different reasoning path reaching the same conclusion, not noise.

So the honest verdict is two claims and they must not be collapsed:

- **The graded result survives.** By the gate as registered - 13/13 AND every
  answer string unchanged - **MTP graduates, with n=4 the operating point.**
- **E57's determinism property does not.** We can no longer say this model
  reproduces byte-identically under this config. The `strict_identical` check
  was added before results were seen and measures something the registered gate
  did not ask about, so it is reported beside the verdict rather than folded
  into it. The gate is not moved in either direction.

**A deployment concern the speed figure hides:** at n=2, `F1` used 41% fewer
tokens for the same answer. If that generalises, part of MTP's benefit is
SHORTER REASONING rather than faster tokens - a quality change wearing a
performance costume. Stage 2 measures token count explicitly for that reason.

## E60 (E59 stage 2): does MTP make the chat tier fast enough to remove routing? (2026-08-19, pre-registered before any run)

Four cells, chat tier only, 27B at `reasoning_effort: off`, n=4 fixed. E59
earned the right to drop n=2, other quants and other backends from this
experiment.

| MTP | profile | role |
|---|---|---|
| off | balanced | the existing **5.48s** control |
| n=4 | balanced | **primary architecture test** |
| off | performance | profile main effect |
| n=4 | performance | interaction / best attainable |

**Acceptance is measured again, not inherited.** E59's 83.4% is on held-out legal
reasoning at `low`. Acceptance depends on the draft sequence actually proposed,
and short conversational continuations are a different prediction problem, so
stage 2 measures its own.

### Three outcomes, kept separate

1. **Registered falsifier.** If `MTP n=4 + balanced` is **under 2.0s warm
   median**, the two-model recommendation is falsified by its original rule.
   **Balanced is the condition for this test** because that is where the 5.48s
   measurement and the rule were established - letting a profile change into the
   falsifier would move the goalposts silently.
2. **Operational decision, which is NOT the falsifier.** At 2.3-2.8s the
   falsifier stays unfired, and the separate question gets asked explicitly: is
   saving 1.5-2s per chat response worth a second resident model and a routing
   layer? That is engineering judgement, not an experimental result.
3. **Best-hardware result.** If only `performance + MTP` crosses 2s, it is
   recorded as its own claim: single-model chat latency is viable under the
   performance power policy but not under the historical balanced one.

### Predictions

1. **PRIMARY: `MTP n=4 + balanced` does NOT go below 2.0s.** Expected band
   **2.3-3.1s**, centre near 2.6s.
2. **`performance` helps less than MTP does**, and the two do not multiply
   cleanly.
3. **Chat/off MTP-4 acceptance >= 83%** - short conversational continuations
   should be easier to predict than long legal reasoning. **Falsified if under
   83%.**
4. **TOKEN-COUNT INVARIANCE: MTP does not change median generated tokens on
   chat/off by more than 10%.** If it does, the latency gain is a compound
   behavioural-plus-inference effect and must be reported as one rather than as
   a hardware optimisation.
5. **Decode speedup on chat is at least the 2.08x E59 measured on legal text**,
   given prediction 3.

### Decomposition recorded per cell

Warm median wall, TTFT/prompt-processing split (`timings.prompt_ms`), generated
tokens, measured generation tok/s, draft acceptance, accepted drafts per
verification, effective tokens per verification, and latency normalised to the
vanilla answer length. The normalisation exists to separate *MTP decoded faster*
from *MTP emitted fewer tokens*, which E59's `F1` proved is a real distinction.

**Note on execution:** `powerprofilesctl set` is polkit-denied for agent-spark,
so the two `performance` cells require the owner to switch the profile. The two
`balanced` cells run now; the profile is RECORDED in every result file rather
than assumed.

## E60 RESULTS (2026-08-19): MTP is worth 2x on documents and 1.3x on chat, because ACCEPTANCE is a property of the workload

| chat tier, 27B `off` | balanced | performance | profile effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| MTP off | 5.34s | 5.31s | +0.6% |
| **MTP n=4** | **4.05s** | **4.04s** | +0.2% |
| MTP effect | **1.32x** | **1.31x** | - |

**The registered falsifier did not fire: 4.05s against 2.0s.** The two-model
recommendation stands, by a wider margin than the projection suggested.

**The power profile does nothing measurable.** 0.6% and 0.2%, inside run-to-run
noise, and the MTP effect is identical under both policies (1.32x vs 1.31x).
Prediction 2 held in its strongest form - not "helps less than MTP" but "does
not help". **That branch is closed**: there is no reason to revisit power policy
for inference on this box, and the fact that every previously published figure
was measured under `balanced` costs nothing.

### Predictions: two held, three falsified, and all three falsifications have ONE cause

| # | prediction | result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | MTP n=4 + balanced not below 2.0s, band 2.3-3.1s | direction right, **band FALSIFIED** at 4.05s |
| 2 | `performance` helps less than MTP, no clean multiplication | **HELD** |
| 3 | chat/off acceptance >= 83% | **FALSIFIED** at 30.2% |
| 4 | token-count invariance within 10% | **HELD exactly**, 57 tokens in all four cells |
| 5 | chat decode speedup >= E59's 2.08x | **FALSIFIED** at 1.32x |

**F85. Draft acceptance is a property of the WORKLOAD, not of the model, the
backend or the hardware.** Same GGUF, same build, same Vulkan device, same
`--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 4`:

| workload | acceptance | accepted/verification | decode gain |
|---|---|---|---|
| held-out legal reasoning at `low` (E59) | **83.4%** | 3.34 | **2.08x** |
| short conversational prose at `off` (E60) | **30.2%** | 1.21 | **1.32x** |

The direction is the opposite of what was registered. Formulaic legal answers -
structured citations, templated phrasing, a fixed two-line response shape - are
easy for a draft head to predict. Free-form explanatory prose is not. **A
speculative-decoding speedup measured on one workload does not transfer to
another**, and 30.2% is below the 60% threshold at which speculation is
generally held to pay for itself at all.

The 30.2% reproduced to the decimal on the `performance` arm, an independent run
at a different power policy, so it is not a sampling artefact - though the chat
sample is 168 draft events against the legal conversation's 1,398, so the figure
should not be quoted to a decimal.

**This was the caveat that carried the experiment.** E59's acceptance was
deliberately not inherited. Inheriting 83.4% would have projected roughly 2.6s;
the measured answer is 4.05s. The architecture argument would have been wrong by
1.4 seconds.

### Token-count invariance held exactly, and it scopes the E59 concern

**57 generated tokens in all four cells**, a 0.0% change. So on chat the 1.32x
is pure inference gain with no behavioural component. The "quality change
wearing a performance costume" worry from E59 - where `F1` used 41% fewer tokens
for the same answer - appeared **only in the long legal conversation at
`reasoning_effort: low`**, not in short chat at `off`. That is a scope, not a
general property, and any future MTP decision should re-check it per workload
rather than assume either result.

### What this settles operationally

**Enable MTP for document work; on chat the gain is real but does not change the
routing decision.** 5.34s to 4.05s is a 24% latency reduction, which is not
nothing - it is simply far short of what a routing change would need. 2.08x with
answers unchanged on legal reasoning, against 1.32x with acceptance below the
threshold on chat. That is a routing conclusion in its own right, and it aligns
with the two-model design rather than cutting against it, because the 27B is
where document work already goes.

Machine facts unchanged from the E59 table. The `performance` arms were run by
the owner switching the profile (polkit denies agent-spark), and the profile was
restored to `balanced` afterwards; every result file records the profile it ran
under rather than assuming it.

## E61: can a different MoE close the hard-tier gap, or is the split DENSE vs SPARSE? (2026-08-19, pre-registered before any run)

**The question.** The workhorse scores **5/12** on the L3 hard tier where
Qwen3.8-27B scores **12/12**. Two models already on hand test whether a
different MoE closes that, without a download:

| model | arch | what it tests |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-30B-A3B (workhorse) | MoE, ~3B active | existing baseline, **5/12** |
| **GLM-4.7-Flash** | MLA, 30B-A3B class | can another small-active MoE improve hard reasoning? |
| **gpt-oss-120b** | MoE, 117B total / ~5.1B active | does much larger TOTAL capacity help despite tiny active set? |
| Qwen3.8-27B | dense | quality ceiling, **12/12** |

**Both candidates are already downloaded and manifest-recorded.** GLM-4.7-Flash
is live on sparkmax; gpt-oss-120b (59.03 GiB, 3 shards, SHA256 pinned, fetched
2026-07-03) is on sparkline's backup store. No new downloads gate this.

**Speed is ignored on the first pass** beyond checking it is not catastrophic.
This tier is about whether the capability exists at all.

### What is already known, and why it lowers but does not settle the prior

gpt-oss-120b has been measured on speed and writing, never on knowledge work:
**53.44 tg128, 48.35 tg@8K, drafting 3.00, MMLU 72.7%** - and that MMLU is
BELOW the workhorse's 80.2%. GLM-4.7-Flash has architecture findings (F8: it
runs the deepseek2/MLA graph; F11, F18: MLA anti-scales under concurrency) and
a drafting score of 3.10, but has **never been run on any knowledge-work tier**.

MMLU is not the failure being measured. L3-hard is much closer to it, so a low
MMLU lowers the prior without deciding anything.

### Registered decision bands, applied to BOTH candidates

- **10-12/12** - serious reviewer candidate. Proceed to an E57-style held-out
  run and to latency.
- **8-9/12** - interesting middle tier, worth pursuing ONLY if latency is
  compelling.
- **7/12 or below** - not enough gain over the workhorse to justify another
  resident model. Close the candidate.

### Predictions

1. **PRIMARY: gpt-oss-120b scores 7/12 or below**, i.e. lands in the closing
   band. Its MMLU is below the workhorse's and the L3 failure is about holding
   implicit constraints together, which total parameter count may not buy.
2. **GLM-4.7-Flash scores 5-8/12** - better than the workhorse but well short of
   the 27B.
3. **Neither reaches 10/12.**
4. **The failures cluster on the SAME questions the workhorse misses** -
   precedence and multi-hop.

**The falsifier that would change the architecture: either candidate at 10/12 or
above.** That would mean a fast sparse model can do the work the dense 27B is
resident for, and the routing decision reopens.

**The counter-argument, registered because it is the more likely finding.** If
BOTH candidates fail in roughly the same places as the workhorse, the useful
conclusion is that **the dense-versus-sparse split matters more than choosing a
better MoE**. That closes the whole MoE-hunting branch and promotes the cascade
experiment - workhorse drafts, 27B audits and corrects, measured on total
elapsed time to a correct answer - to the front of the queue. A negative result
here is therefore worth as much as a positive one.

**Cost.** Two arms on an existing 12-question tier, local, no cloud spend.
gpt-oss-120b at 59.03 GiB is NEAR-EDGE for the amdgpu suballocator deadlock
(`docs/memory-edge-deadlock.md`): it must be loaded with the box quiet, with no
concurrent download, backup or hashing, and with someone able to power-cycle.
The backup and any downloads complete FIRST, and nothing overlaps that load.

### E61 GLM CONFIRMATION: the decision rule, registered BEFORE the arm runs (2026-08-19 06:28)

Written while the `max_tokens 16384` arm is still queued and unrun, because a
budget that gets reinterpreted after seeing the score is a moving target.

GLM-4.7-Flash scored **10/12** at `max_tokens 4096`. Both misses - `P1`
(precedence) and `Z1` (underspecified) - hit `finish_reason: length` at exactly
4,096 generated tokens. They are truncations, **not demonstrated wrong answers**,
which means 10/12 **may underestimate** what GLM can achieve. It does not mean
the true score is higher: a completed answer can still be wrong.

**The rule:**

1. **If both truncated cases complete CORRECTLY at 16,384 tokens**, the 4,096
   result was budget-limited. GLM earns latency testing against the real traffic
   mix **immediately**, ahead of GPT-OSS-120B.
2. **If either completes INCORRECTLY**, that is a capability result. Retain the
   resulting 10/12 or 11/12 and apply the existing decision bands **without
   reinterpretation** - no further budget raises, no "it was nearly right".
3. **Either way the 4,096 figure remains the headline** for comparison against
   the workhorse's 5/12 and the 27B's 12/12, because that is the budget all three
   were measured at.

**And if GLM reaches 12/12, it is NOT thereby equivalent to the dense 27B.** The
next instrument is E57's held-out depth design, not another single-turn tier.
E57 is precisely the experiment that showed a strong single-turn result
disappearing when the context structure changed - Qwen3-8B held 5 of 5 anchors
with its own answer in view and lost 4 of 10 without it. A sparse model matching
12/12 on one hard tier would be an excellent result and would still say nothing
about whether it holds up across a long conversation.

## F86 - model evaluation and SYSTEM evaluation are different measurements, and ranking models produces wrong engineering answers

Recorded 2026-08-19 as the session's most transferable output. Five results from
this programme, each of which a model-ranking table gets wrong:

| observation | what ranking models would conclude | what is actually true |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-8B: 41.6 tok/s, second-fastest arm | fast model | **slowest but one to a user** - 9.46s, because it emits 394 tokens where the 27B emits 57 |
| MTP on Qwen3.8-27B | "MTP is worth 2.08x" | **2.08x on structured legal work, 1.32x on chat** - same model, same flag, same hardware |
| gpt-oss-120b: 117B total against the workhorse's 30B | more capacity, better answers | **MMLU 72.7% vs 80.2%** and no evidence either way on the hard-tier failures that actually matter |
| GLM-4.7-Flash: 10/12 | a 10/12 model | **cannot yet distinguish capability failure from budget exhaustion** |
| workhorse: 5/12 on L3-hard | too weak for document work | **may be an excellent first stage** in a system whose answer is checked by the 27B |

**The hierarchy this implies, and the order matters:**

```
model metrics  ->  workload metrics  ->  task outcome  ->  system cost
```

Each level can invert the one before it. A model metric (tok/s) inverted at the
workload level (the 8B). A workload metric (2.08x decode) failed to transfer
across workloads (MTP on chat). A task outcome may yet invert a capability score
(the workhorse at 5/12 as a drafting stage).

**`tok/s` becomes actively misleading the moment cascades enter.** A two-call
system can generate fewer tokens per second in aggregate and still reach a
trustworthy answer sooner, if the expensive model only has to inspect and repair
a concise draft rather than write one. Any cascade instrument must therefore
measure **total elapsed time to a correct answer, counting every call**, and
never a per-model rate.

**These are DESIGN PRINCIPLES, not conclusions.** Their use is to settle what
the next experiment should measure whenever there is ambiguity. The question is
not *which model wins* but **which arrangement reaches a trustworthy answer
fastest and most economically.**

- The useful unit of optimisation is the **workload**, not the model.
- The useful unit of architecture is the **task outcome**, not the model call.

### E61 gpt-oss-120b: the smoke test's interpretation, registered BEFORE it runs (2026-08-19)

The arm is **UNRUN**. Its 0/12 is twelve `transport_failed` outcomes - a
transport failure before the model produced any evaluable answer is
**infrastructure evidence, not model-quality evidence** - and must never be
quoted as a capability score. Detail: `docs/2026-08-19-gptoss120b-decode-hang.md`.

`tools/smoke_first_token.py`: one ten-token prompt, `max_tokens 32`, hard
timeout, **streaming** so time-to-first-token is stamped separately from total
request time. TTFT is the measurement here, not the response - if loading
succeeds, prompt evaluation succeeds, and the first sampled token never appears,
the boundary is narrowed considerably.

**The four branches, and what each does and does NOT support:**

1. **No generated token before the timeout** -> supports a first-decode /
   backend stall. **It does not by itself prove Vulkan/RADV is the cause.** A GPU
   fence wait is a plausible mechanism; the externally observed symptom is a
   stalled decode and nothing more. Do not write a mechanism into the record that
   was not measured.
2. **Tokens arrive but generation never terminates** -> supports the
   reasoning/runaway branch, the F71 shape (Qwen3.8 at `xhigh` burning 100,000
   tokens over 2h 46m and emitting nothing).
3. **32 tokens complete normally** -> the failure is INTERMITTENT or
   workload/context dependent. **Only then** is a slightly larger reproduction
   justified.
4. **The process exits or crashes** -> preserve stderr, the serverlog, exit
   status and the amdgpu kernel messages BEFORE another attempt. agent-spark
   cannot read the kernel ring buffer, so `dmesg | grep -i amdgpu` is an owner
   action.

**Priority is explicitly subordinate to GLM.** If GLM's confirmation completes
both truncated cases correctly, the strategic value of debugging gpt-oss drops
sharply. If GLM fails one or both, getting gpt-oss to emit a first token becomes
considerably more valuable. The two must not be allowed to masquerade as each
other:

> **GLM's confirmation decides architecture priority. The gpt-oss smoke test
> diagnoses infrastructure. Neither result is evidence of the other kind.**

Which is the general form of what this session keeps re-learning: **before asking
how well the model performed, establish that you measured the model at all.**

## E61 GLM RESULT (2026-08-19): 10/12 with two NON-TERMINATING reasoning failures

**GLM-4.7-Flash scores 10/12 on the hard tier, with two non-terminating
reasoning failures that persist from 4,096 to 16,384 output tokens.**

That wording is deliberate. It keeps capability and robustness separate, and it
makes clear that the larger budget **falsified** the "it just needed more room"
interpretation rather than confirming it.

| budget | score | wall | P1 | Z1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `max_tokens 4096` | 10/12 | 423.9s | truncated, 4,096 gen | truncated, 4,096 gen |
| `max_tokens 16384` | **10/12** | 1001.2s | **truncated, 16,384 gen** | **truncated, 16,384 gen** |

Every other cell identical. Wall time 2.4x, entirely from the two runaways.

**The shape matters more than the score.** The ten successful answers use a
**median of 1,365** generated tokens. P1 and Z1 reach **16,384 without producing
an answer** - **exactly 12.0x** the median. That is not a modest long-tail
effect; it is a distinct failure mode.

**Reasoning volume on the two:** 68,016 and 65,662 characters, and no answer.

**Correction 2026-08-19 (median restated 1,373 -> 1,365).** The ten completed
answers are 898, 1006, 1077, 1162, 1357, 1373, 1640, 1661, 1946, 2328. With an
even sample the median is the mean of the 5th and 6th values, **1,365**; 1,373 is
the upper-middle element - `sorted[n//2]` on an even-length list. It changes the
headline ratio in the finding's favour: `16384/1365` is **12.00x exactly**, where
`16384/1373` is 11.93x, so "at least 12x" was true only on the corrected figure.
Recomputed from `results/raw/e61-20260819-glm47flash-l3n0{,-budget16k}.json`;
both arms carry the identical ten completions, which is itself the
bit-determinism of F88.

### Against the registered rule: reality produced a THIRD branch

The rule registered before the run had two branches - both complete correctly
(budget-limited), or either completes incorrectly (capability result). Neither
fits: **neither completed at all.** Rule 2's operative clause is applied
unchanged - **10/12 stands, and no further budget raises** - and the rule is NOT
retrofitted to claim it anticipated this.

**A precision the score does not carry:** capability on P1 and Z1 is
**UNMEASURED, not demonstrated-absent.** The model never committed, so whether
it could have reached the right answer is unknown. "10/12 with 2
non-terminating" is a stronger and more defensible claim than a bare 10/12, and
is the form that should be quoted.

### The qualitative pattern, labelled as a pattern from two cases

`P1` is **precedence**; `Z1` is **underspecified**. Both require **committing
under conflict or ambiguity**. Failing to terminate on exactly those two, while
finishing ten others at a 1,365-token median, is not a knowledge failure - it is
**a failure to terminate deliberation when there is no clean resolution.**

This is a pattern from two cases, not a general theorem, and must be quoted that
way.

**For a reviewer role it is pointed.** "These two rules conflict" is a NORMAL
input for a reviewer, not an edge case. The practical phrasing:

> GLM showed strong capability on most hard items, but on the two questions that
> required committing under conflict or ambiguity it failed to terminate even
> with a 4x larger token budget. That makes it risky as an **unattended**
> reviewer unless a watchdog and fallback are part of the design.

That says why the failure matters operationally without claiming it "cannot
reason about conflict", which the evidence does not support.

### The counterpoint, which must not be lost

**10/12 is still materially stronger than the workhorse's 5/12 on this tier.**
E61 rules out GLM as a **dependable unattended reviewer without a watchdog**. It
does NOT rule out GLM as a useful specialist for bounded workloads where a hard
generation cap and a fallback route are acceptable. Do not discard it.

### Three things to carry forward as METRICS

1. **Non-termination rate is a first-class robustness metric**, tracked
   alongside correctness. A wrong answer is detectable downstream; a reviewer
   that sometimes enters a 16K-token loop becomes the bottleneck for the whole
   task.
2. **A stopping rule for future diagnostics:** if an item exceeds roughly **4-6x
   the model's median successful generation length** without reaching an answer,
   treat it as a runaway candidate and terminate rather than assuming more budget
   helps. **NOT applied retroactively to the published GLM score** - it is a
   time-saver for later work, not a re-scoring.
3. **Commitment latency**, a metric this programme does not yet have. Total
   tokens and wall time cannot distinguish a model taking a long time because
   the task is genuinely long from one consuming thousands of tokens without
   ever crossing from deliberation into an answer. P1 and Z1 are the latter.
   Even a crude proxy - *reasoning tokens before the first answer-bearing
   sentence* - would be valuable for comparing reviewer candidates.

## E61 gpt-oss-120b: the bisect - the original failure is INTERMITTENT and remains UNEXPLAINED

The smoke test completed normally: **TTFT 0.98s**, 31 chunks, 1.5s. That killed
both registered hypotheses - no first-decode stall, no runaway - and selected
branch 3: workload/context dependent, so a larger reproduction was justified.

`tools/bisect_hang.py` walked five rungs **inside one model load**, moving one
variable at a time from the condition known to work toward the condition known
to fail. Loading once removes load-to-load variation as a confound and spends
the wall clock on requests rather than on reloading a model that already works.

| rung | condition | result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | tiny prompt, `max_tokens 32` | ok, ttft 0.88s |
| 2 | tiny prompt, `max_tokens 4096` | ok, ttft 0.16s |
| 3 | 4,000-char prompt, `max_tokens 32` | ok, ttft 2.44s |
| 4 | real 13,393-char pack, `max_tokens 32` | ok, ttft 8.57s |
| **5** | **real pack, `max_tokens 4096` - the failing condition** | **ok, ttft 0.15s, 305 chunks, 6.4s** |

**NO rung stalled, including the full failing condition.**

Applying the interpretation rules exactly as registered:

- **The original failure remains intermittent and unexplained.**
- **The walk succeeding does NOT retroactively make the first failure "not
  real".** Twelve `transport_failed` outcomes happened and the serverlog stopped
  mid-decode.
- A rung failing would have identified **the condition that exposes** the
  failure, not the root cause; none did, so not even that is available.
- It remains **infrastructure evidence, not model-quality evidence**.

Rung 5 satisfies the "single hard-tier item before committing to all 12" gate -
real pack, real question shape, the full answer budget - so the 12-question
re-run follows.

## The evidence-class distinction, which is now the session's organising idea

**Failures of COMPLETION, TRANSPORT, CORRECTNESS and LATENCY are different
evidence classes and must not collapse into one score.** This session produced
one of each:

| class | instance | what it is NOT |
|---|---|---|
| transport | gpt-oss 12x `transport_failed` | not a 0/12 capability score |
| completion | GLM P1/Z1 non-terminating | not a wrong answer; capability there is unmeasured |
| correctness | GLM 10/12, workhorse 5/12 | not a statement about speed or reliability |
| latency | 27B 5.48s vs workhorse 0.91s chat | not a statement about quality |

**A model can have good capability and still be a poor system component because
of its failure mode.** That is exactly what a leaderboard cannot show, and it is
the sharpest form of F86 this session produced.

## E61 gpt-oss-120b RESULT (2026-08-19): 12/12 - the dense/sparse split is NOT the limiting factor

The 12-question re-run, after the smoke test and the five-rung bisect established
the earlier failure was intermittent infrastructure rather than model behaviour.

| arm | score | wall | median gen | non-terminating |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| workhorse 30B-A3B | 5/12 | **14.1s** | 23 | 0 |
| GLM-4.7-Flash | 10/12 | 423.9s | 1,640 | **2** |
| **gpt-oss-120b** | **12/12** | **178.7s** | 392 | 0 |
| Qwen3.8-27B (dense) | 12/12 | 485.6s | 401 | 0 |

**gpt-oss-120b matches the dense 27B's score at 2.7x the speed**, with
near-identical median generation (392 vs 401 tokens), citations 12/12, and zero
non-termination. Per-question wall: min 4.38s, median 13.28s, max 27.22s.

### Predictions: the primary one was decisively falsified

1. **PRIMARY - gpt-oss-120b scores 7/12 or below. FALSIFIED at 12/12.** The
   reasoning behind it - MMLU 72.7% against the workhorse's 80.2%, and total
   capacity not necessarily buying the specific failure being measured - was
   sound as a prior and simply wrong. MMLU did not predict this tier.
2. **GLM 5-8/12. FALSIFIED** at 10/12.
3. **Neither reaches 10/12. FALSIFIED twice over.**
4. **Failures cluster on the same questions the workhorse misses. VOID** - one
   candidate had no failures at all.

**The registered counter-argument is REJECTED.** It said that if both candidates
failed in the same places, the dense-versus-sparse split would matter more than
choosing a better MoE, and the MoE-hunting branch should close. Instead a sparse
model with roughly 5.1B active parameters matched the dense model exactly.
**Sparsity is not the limiting factor**, and the branch closes in the opposite
direction from the one anticipated.

### What this does NOT establish

- **ONE run**, and the immediately preceding run of the **identical
  configuration** failed entirely with 12x `transport_failed`
  (`docs/2026-08-19-gptoss120b-decode-hang.md`, still unexplained). **Not
  load-bearing until repeated.**
- **Capability only.** Robustness (E57 held-out depth), efficiency (real traffic
  latency) and system value are all open - the F86 four questions, three of them
  unanswered.
- `distractors=0` only. F74's scaling behaviour is unmeasured for this model.

### Why the diagnostic sequence mattered

Had the first run's 0/12 been recorded as a capability score, this model would
have been discarded as hopeless. It is instead the joint-best arm on the tier.
The distinction between transport failure and model quality (F87) was worth
exactly one model in this instance.

## R&D PROGRAMME PROPOSED (2026-08-19)

Five hypotheses with falsifiers, a research tree in which every negative result
buys something, and **TTCA - Time To Correct Answer** replacing `tok/s` as the
headline metric:
`docs/plans/2026-08-19-rd-programme-inference-as-resource-allocation.md`

The proposition: **effective inference is a resource-allocation problem, not a
model-selection problem.** Not *which local model is best*, but *given a fixed
hardware and latency budget, where should inference compute be spent to maximise
the probability of a correct, completed answer?*

## E62: does gpt-oss-120b's 12/12 REPRODUCE? (2026-08-19, pre-registered before the run)

**Why this and nothing else first.** E61 recorded gpt-oss-120b at **12/12** on
L3-hard in 178.7s. That is ONE run, and the *identical* configuration - same
binary (`llama.cpp/wt/b10435`), same shards, same flags - failed entirely
immediately before it: twelve `transport_failed` from a decode hang that is
still unexplained (`docs/2026-08-19-gptoss120b-decode-hang.md`). A single run
from a configuration with a demonstrated intermittent fault is not a
load-bearing capability result, and every downstream question in the R&D
programme (robustness, efficiency, system value) is priced off it.

**Design.** Exact repeat, nothing varied: `--tier l3 --distractors 0
--max-tokens 4096 --ctx 32768 --thinking default`, same `--server-bin`. The only
difference is a fresh server process and a fresh label.

### Predictions

1. **PRIMARY: 12/12 again, all twelve questions completing (`finish_reason:
   stop`, zero `transport_failed`).** E61's run was clean throughout - no
   truncation, no transport error - and the hang struck at first decode, not
   mid-run.
2. **Every answer byte-identical to E61's.** Temperature is fixed and E57
   already showed this model class reproducing byte-for-byte across separate
   processes.
3. **Wall time within +/-15% of 178.7s** (152 - 206s).
4. **The decode hang does NOT recur.** It has been observed once in three loads
   of this model today.

**Falsifiers, and what each would mean:**

- **Any score below 12/12 on a completed run** - E61's 12/12 was not a stable
  property of the model and the headline must be re-stated as a range, not a
  figure. This is the result that would most change the programme.
- **A recurrence of the decode hang** - the intermittency is frequent enough to
  disqualify gpt-oss-120b from any unattended role regardless of its score, and
  diagnosis stops being optional. Record it as an instrument failure, NOT as a
  capability score (the E61 rule stands).
- **Answers differing while the score holds** - determinism is not a property of
  this arm, so per-question cells are not reproducible and only the aggregate is
  citable (the F76 treatment).

**Cost.** One arm, ~3 minutes of run plus a 59.03 GiB load. Near-edge for the
amdgpu suballocator deadlock: box quiet, no concurrent download, backup or
hashing, run attended.

**12/12 again, and all four predictions held.** Not merely the same score - the
same computation.

| | E61 retry | E62 repeat |
|---|---|---|
| score | 12/12 | **12/12** |
| citations valid | 12/12 | 12/12 |
| over-claims | 0/1 | 0/1 |
| wall | 178.7s | **178.0s** (-0.4%) |

## E63: does gpt-oss-120b hold up at DEPTH, or only in single turns? (2026-08-19, pre-registered before any run)

**Prerequisite 2 of the R&D programme.** E62 closed capability: 12/12 on
L3-hard, reproduced bit-for-bit. F88 states plainly what that does not buy - a
deterministic arm reproduces its errors as faithfully as its successes, so
nothing about robustness follows from it. E57 is the instrument that already
caught this exact illusion once: **Qwen3-8B held 5 of 5 anchors with its own
answer in the history and lost 4 of 10 when the questions were held out.**

**Design: E57's crossover, unchanged.** Two runs over the same L4 pack,
`heldout-ab` and `heldout-ba`, each question asked exactly once per run, so the
model's own earlier answer is never in the context it re-reads. 18 turns, 13
graded, probes split shallow / recent / deep.

**Serving assumption, stated because it is a choice.** `--thinking default`,
`--ctx 32768`, `--max-tokens 5120`, matching E57's arms on context and budget
and matching E62 on the reasoning setting. `default` is the setting under which
this model scored 12/12; changing it here would confound depth with reasoning
budget. The comparison arms (Qwen3.8-27B at `low`, Qwen3-8B, workhorse) are
already run and are NOT re-run.

### Predictions

1. **PRIMARY: gpt-oss-120b scores 12-13/13 on each arm** with **no deep
   degradation** - deep probes within 1 of shallow probes. It matched the dense
   27B exactly on L3-hard, and the 27B is the arm that held 10/10 shallow and
   10/10 deep.
2. **`wrong_document` is 0 on both arms.** It has been 0 on every arm of every
   conversation experiment so far (F74's conversational analogue), and this
   model was 0 over-claims on L3-hard.
3. **Both arms complete with no `transport_failed`.** Two further loads; four
   consecutive clean ones precede them.
4. **Wall per arm under 400s**, from E61's 2.7x speed advantage over the dense
   27B, whose E57 arm was 695.9s.

**Falsifiers, and what each means:**

- **Deep probes 2 or more below shallow on either arm** - the capability is
  single-turn only, gpt-oss-120b joins the 8B in F83's amendment, and it is
  disqualified as a reviewer over a long context regardless of its L3-hard
  score. **This is the result that would most change the programme**, and it is
  a live possibility: ~5.1B active parameters is the 8B's order of magnitude,
  not the 27B's.
- **Any `wrong_document`** - the first non-zero in this programme, and it would
  make the model unsafe on a folder of similar agreements, which is the actual
  deployment shape.
- **A decode hang on either load** - recorded as instrument failure, NOT a
  capability score (the E61 rule stands), and the hang denominator becomes 1 in 6
  or 1 in 7 rather than 1 in 5.

**Cost.** Two arms, two 59.03 GiB loads, no cloud spend. Near-edge for the
amdgpu suballocator deadlock: box quiet, run attended.

### E63 RESULT: depth is NOT the weakness - the failure is a flat, position-independent off-by-one (2026-08-19 08:14)

**All four predictions held.** Both arms clean, no `transport_failed`, no hang.

| | arm ab | arm ba |
|---|---|---|
| score | 12/13 | 12/13 |
| wall | 234.9s | 215.4s |
| shallow | 5/5 | 4/5 |
| recent | 3/3 | 3/3 |
| deep | 4/5 | 5/5 |
| `wrong_document` | 0 | 0 |
| `accepted_false` | 0 | 0 |

**Joined across the crossover, which is the measurement:**

```
shallow 9/10  ->  deep 9/10   at 22,066 of 32,768 tokens (67.3%)
degraded: none    improved: none    wrong_document at depth: none
recent probes: 6/6
```

**The single failure is the same question in both positions, with the same wrong
answer.** `P3` is `off_by_calendar` shallow AND deep - **15 September 2026**
where the answer is 14 September 2026. Because the crossover asks each question
exactly once per run and swaps which run asks it early, a question wrong in both
positions is wrong independently of depth. **Depth is exonerated.**

**What the error actually is, and it is not a retrieval failure.** `P3` plants
three candidate trigger dates in `CHRON` on purpose - the breach, the discovery,
and the earlier contract - and STAT-LIM paragraph 2 names which one governs.
Choosing another grades as `wrong_trigger`. gpt-oss-120b did **not** do that: it
selected the correct trigger and then landed on the `+1 day` trap. It read the
documents correctly and computed the last day of the period wrongly, by one day -
an inclusive/exclusive boundary error on a limitation period.

**Every other arm gets this question right**, at both depths: Qwen3.8-27B,
Qwen3-8B, and the workhorse all answer 14 September 2026 deep. (The workhorse
fails it *shallow*, as `wrong_trigger` - a different error entirely, and the
reason F80's tiering says use it to read a contract and never to work out a
date.) gpt-oss-120b is the only arm to make this particular mistake.

**More reasoning did not buy correctness, and this is the datum prerequisite 4
wants.** The same wrong answer cost **1,679** reasoning characters shallow and
**5,367** deep - 3.2x the reasoning for an identical wrong output. Reasoning
volume is not evidence of reasoning quality, and a commitment-latency proxy built
on reasoning length must not assume otherwise.

**Predictions, scored:**

1. 12-13/13 per arm with deep within 1 of shallow - **HELD**, and more strongly
   than registered: the gap is 0, not 1.
2. `wrong_document` 0 on both arms - **HELD**
3. no `transport_failed` - **HELD**
4. wall per arm under 400s - **HELD** at 234.9s and 215.4s

**Hang denominator: one in seven loads** on 2026-08-19 (failed L3 run, smoke,
bisect, E61 retry, E62, E63 ab, E63 ba). Six consecutive clean loads now. Still
no rate, still unexplained, still disqualifying for unattended use.

Evidence: `results/raw/e63-20260819-gptoss120b-heldout-{ab,ba}.json`,
`results/raw/e63-gptoss120b-paired.json`.

## E64: what does gpt-oss-120b cost on the REAL traffic mix? (2026-08-19, pre-registered before any run)

**Prerequisite 3, the efficiency question.** E62 established capability (12/12,
reproduced bit-for-bit) and E63 established robustness (shallow 9/10 -> deep
9/10, no degradation). Neither says what it costs to answer, and F86's ordering
is explicit: capability -> robustness -> efficiency -> system value. A model that
passes the first two and takes 30 seconds on a chat turn has no route.

**The instrument is E58's, unchanged**, over the three tiers built from 952 real
relay requests: `chat` (91.3% of traffic, median 68 prompt tokens),
`document` (the 3.9% between), `folder` (the 1.4% carrying 34% of generation
time).

**Comparability, stated rather than assumed.** gpt-oss-120b runs ALONE as a new
`--arm-set gptoss`, and is compared against the **banked** E58 residency figures
rather than re-running them. Same day, same kernel (`7.0.0-28-generic`), same
server binary (`llama.cpp/wt/b10435`), same `--server-extra -b 512 -ub 128`,
same `--ctx 32768`, same tier definitions. Re-running the other four would spend
~15 minutes of GPU reproducing figures already pinned and would create a second
measurement of them to reconcile. **The one condition that differs from E62/E63
is `-b 512 -ub 128`**, which those runs did not use - so these latency numbers
are not directly comparable to E62's 178.0s wall, and that is by design: this
arm must match E58, not E62.

### The numbers it is measured against (E58, warm medians)

| arm | chat | document | folder |
|---|---|---|---|
| workhorse 30B-A3B | **0.91s** | 0.38s | 0.29s |
| Qwen3.8-27B `off` | 5.48s | 3.20s | 1.77s |
| Qwen3.8-27B `low` | 22.15s | 16.54s | 50.10s |
| Qwen3-8B | 9.46s | 8.61s | 51.29s |

### Predictions

1. **PRIMARY: chat warm median between 3s and 8s** - slower than the workhorse
   by a wide margin, in the same band as the 27B at `off`. E61 put it at 2.7x
   the dense 27B's wall on L3-hard, but that tier rewards its lower token count;
   chat is where E58 showed token COUNT dominating token RATE.
2. **It does not beat 0.91s on chat**, so it does not displace the workhorse as
   the resident model. The two-model architecture stands.
3. **Median generated tokens on chat between 50 and 250** - it emitted 392
   median on L3-hard, well below GLM's 1,640, and E58's lesson is that a model
   that will not stop is slow regardless of its rate.
4. **Cold load over 100s.** 59.03 GiB off disk; the 27B's folder cold was
   100.71s at a quarter the weight.

**Falsifiers, and what each means:**

- **Chat warm median under 2.0s** - it becomes a candidate RESIDENT model, not
  just a reviewer, and the architecture question reopens for the first time
  since E60 closed it. This is the result that would most change the programme.
- **Chat warm median over 15s** - it is unusable on 91.3% of traffic and its
  role narrows to the offline folder tier only, whatever its capability.
- **A decode hang on this load** - instrument failure, not a latency figure
  (the E61 rule stands), and the denominator becomes 1 in 8.

**Cost.** One arm, three tiers, one 59.03 GiB load. Near-edge for the amdgpu
suballocator deadlock: box quiet, run attended.

### E64 RESULT: 3.66s on chat, and 4-7.7x FASTER than the reasoning arms on real work (2026-08-19 08:17)

| tier | gpt-oss-120b warm | median gen tokens |
|---|---|---|
| chat | **3.66s** | 185 |
| document | **4.14s** | 202 |
| folder | **6.68s** | 260 |

Cold: 4.73s / 17.67s / 117.68s. Model load 22.0s. Full-offload gate passed, 74
layers, all `Vulkan0`. No hang.

**Against the banked E58 arms, and the split is the whole finding.** Two groups,
and reading the table without separating them gives the wrong answer:

**Arms that emit a comparable amount of text** - gpt-oss-120b is much faster:

| | chat | document | folder |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.8-27B `low` | **6.05x slower** | **4.00x slower** | **7.50x slower** |
| Qwen3-8B | **2.58x slower** | **2.08x slower** | **7.68x slower** |

**Arms that emit almost nothing** - gpt-oss-120b is slower, and the comparison is
close to meaningless:

| | chat | document | folder |
|---|---|---|---|
| workhorse 30B-A3B | 0.91s (gen 82) | 0.38s (gen 28) | 0.29s (gen **11**) |
| Qwen3.8-27B `off` | 5.48s (gen 57) | 3.20s (gen 28) | 1.77s (gen **11**) |

**Eleven generated tokens is not an answer to a folder question.** On the tier
carrying 34% of all real generation time, the workhorse and the 27B at `off`
return eleven tokens while gpt-oss-120b returns 260. E58's lesson applied in the
opposite direction: there it was a model looking fast on tok/s and being slow to
a user, here it is models looking fast on wall time by not answering. **Compare
latency only within a band of comparable output volume**, or the number measures
brevity rather than speed.

**The routing answer, and the architecture is unchanged.** gpt-oss-120b does not
displace the workhorse: 3.66s against 0.91s on the 91.3% of traffic that is
chat, so the resident model stays. What it does is beat **every reasoning-capable
arm on every tier**, including 7.50x against the 27B at `low` on the folder tier,
which is precisely the difficult 5% the two-model architecture exists to serve.

**Predictions, scored:**

1. chat warm median 3-8s - **HELD** at 3.66s
2. does not beat 0.91s on chat - **HELD**
3. chat median generated tokens 50-250 - **HELD** at 185
4. "cold load over 100s" - **AMBIGUOUSLY WORDED, and that is a defect in the
   pre-registration rather than a result.** It named the 27B's *folder cold* of
   100.71s as its comparator, and on that reading it held: folder cold is
   117.68s. On the reading "time to load the model" it is falsified: load was
   **22.0s**. Both figures are reported and neither is claimed as a hit.
5. Neither falsifier fired (chat is neither under 2.0s nor over 15s), so the
   architecture question does not reopen and the model is not confined to
   offline work.

**A confound worth recording for anyone comparing load times.** This load took
22.0s where E62's took roughly two minutes for the same 59.03 GiB. The page
cache was warm from E62 and E63 earlier in the session. Model load time on this
box is a statement about the page cache as much as about the model, and
`run_step8_leg.sh`'s missing stack fingerprint does not capture it either.

**Hang denominator: one in eight loads** on 2026-08-19. Seven consecutive clean.

Evidence: `results/raw/e64-20260819-gptoss120b-latency.json`,
`results/raw/latency-20260819.json` (E58, banked).


## E65 - the frontier comparator, and L3-hard is now SATURATED (2026-08-19)

**What was asked:** put Opus through the instruments already built, as the cheap
half of H0 (Opus substitution). **What was actually run is NOT what was asked
for, and that is the first thing to read.**

### The arm is Opus 5 via a subagent harness, NOT Opus 4.7 via API

The owner asked for **Opus 4.7 specifically**. This arm cannot deliver it, for a
reason that is structural rather than an oversight:

- **No working cloud credential exists.** The vaulted
  `SPARKCORE_LLM_OPENROUTER_API_KEY` returns **HTTP 401 `User not found`** on
  both `/api/v1/key` and `/api/v1/credits` - revoked, not merely out of credit
  (that is a 402). No direct Anthropic route exists on this host either: no `ant`
  CLI, no `ANTHROPIC_*` env var, no `anthropic` SDK, no `~/.config/anthropic/`.
- **The subagent transport cannot pin a version.** Claude Code's Agent tool takes
  a model *alias* - `sonnet`/`opus`/`haiku`/`fable` - which resolves to the
  running session's model. That is **Opus 5**, a LATER model than the 4.7 asked
  for.

So this row is a **frontier upper bound**, not the Opus 4.7 measurement. The 4.7
question stays open and is blocked on one owner action: minting a key.

### What was held identical, and what was not

| held identical to E62 | differs |
|---|---|
| the 12 L3-hard questions | transport: one fresh context-free subagent per question, not HTTP to llama-server |
| the pack, asserted at **13,221 chars** | model, obviously |
| the prompt, byte-identical (`PROMPT_TEMPLATE`, no wrapper added) | no token accounting exposed |
| the grader (`grade_answer_l3` + `grade_citation` + `parse_response`) | no serving config, no declared reasoning effort |

Runner: `tools/run_ps_eval_subagent.py`, which writes a `harness_caveats` block
into every result it produces so the file cannot be misread as an API run.

### The result

| arm | L3-hard | citations |
|---|---|---|
| workhorse 30B-A3B | 5/12 | - |
| GLM-4.7-Flash | 10/12 | - |
| gpt-oss-120b | 12/12 | 12/12 |
| Qwen3.8-27B (dense) | 12/12 | 12/12 |
| **Opus 5 (subagent harness)** | **12/12** | **12/12** |

**Contamination guard passed.** The answer key is in
`spikes/ps-eval/questions_l3.py` and the subagents had repo tool access, so this
was a live risk. `tool_uses` is recorded per question and is **0 for all twelve**
- direct evidence none of them went looking. The prompt's own "using ONLY the
engagement pack" instruction was the only guard applied and it was sufficient.

### The finding is about the INSTRUMENT, not the model (F91)

**L3-hard cannot discriminate a frontier model from the two best local arms.**
Three arms now sit at 12/12 with 12/12 citations. As a comparator for H0 the
instrument is **spent**, and no amount of re-running it will produce a number
that separates them.

**What this does NOT say, and the distinction is the whole point.** It does not
say the systems are equal. At n=12 with both arms at ceiling, a true difference
of up to roughly 25 percentage points would still show as 12/12 versus 12/12.
This is the same statistical objection registered against H0's proposed 5pp
threshold in AMENDMENT 2, and it applies to our own result as readily as to
someone else's: **a tie at ceiling is a statement about the ruler.**

### Consequence for H0

Model parity on this tier is answered as far as it can be: **no detectable gap.**
The next instrument must be one where the local arms actually FAIL, and one is
already in hand - E63's `P3`, where gpt-oss-120b picked the right trigger date
and miscounted a six-year deadline by one day, identically in both the shallow
and deep arms, while the 27B, the 8B and the workhorse all got it right. Running
the frontier arm on E57's held-out depth design is the next cheap step, and it
also tests H6 directly.

Evidence: `results/raw/e65-20260819-opus-subagent-l3n0.json` (graded summary +
`harness_caveats`), `results/raw/e65-20260819-opus-subagent-l3n0-answers.json`
(the raw twelve responses).


## E66 - the frontier arm on the held-out depth design: 18/20, the SAME as gpt-oss (2026-08-19)

Follow-on to E65, which established that L3-hard is saturated. This goes where a
local arm demonstrably fails: E63's `P3`.

**Same caveat as E65, and it has not gone away.** The arm is a frontier model
reached through Claude Code subagents, not Opus 4.7 through an API. No working
cloud credential exists and the Agent tool takes a model *alias*, not a version.
Upper bound, not the 4.7 measurement.

### Method

Both crossover orders were driven turn by turn - 18 turns each, one subagent per
arm, continued via SendMessage so the model's OWN answers accumulate in its
context exactly as `run_multiturn_eval.py` builds `messages`. Grading is the
repo's `grade_multiturn` against the same `turn["expect"]` blocks
(`tools/grade_heldout_subagent.py`).

**One deliberate harness difference, declared.** Each turn was delivered as a
FILE PATH for the subagent to read, not pasted inline. The conversation is
103,679 chars per arm and hand-transcribing it risks a silent drop in the middle
of a legal document - an error mode that is invisible and would corrupt
comparability. Reading the file makes the delivered bytes exact. The turn files
live in a scratch directory that contains no answer key; the keys are in
`spikes/ps-eval/`.

### The result

| | AB arm | BA arm | held-out total |
|---|---|---|---|
| **frontier (subagent)** | 12/13 | 12/13 | **18/20** |
| gpt-oss-120b (E63) | 12/13 | 12/13 | **18/20** |

Recent probes R1/R2/R3 correct in both arms (EUR 24,800 / 195,000 / 18,923), so
the deliveries were absorbed. No `wrong_document`, no `accepted_false`, no
non-termination, no transport failure.

### The two arms fail DIFFERENTLY, and that is the whole result

| question | gpt-oss-120b | frontier arm |
|---|---|---|
| `P3` shallow | `off_by_calendar` - **15 September 2026** | `off_by_calendar` - **15 September 2026** |
| `P3` deep | `off_by_calendar` - **15 September 2026** | **correct** - 14 September 2026 |
| `X1` shallow | correct | **wrong** - "YES" where the answer is NO |
| `X1` deep | correct | correct |

**The frontier arm produced the IDENTICAL wrong date to gpt-oss-120b.** Not a
different wrong answer, not a different failure mode - the same six-year
limitation period miscounted by the same one day to the same value. That is the
strongest evidence yet for **H6**: the defect is in the date arithmetic itself,
it is shared across models with nothing else in common, and it is not a
capability gap that a bigger model closes.

**But the frontier arm is NOT deterministic about it.** gpt-oss gave the same
wrong answer in both positions (F88's bit-determinism). This arm was wrong once
and right once on the same question. With **n=1 per cell** that difference cannot
be attributed to position rather than run-to-run variance, and this arm is
demonstrably not deterministic, so the honest reading is *sometimes wrong*, not
*wrong when shallow*.

### The depth axis does NOT transfer, and the deep 10/10 must not be read as robustness

E57/E63 measure degradation when the answer sits far back in a context that is
**67.3% full** (21,694 of 32,768 tokens for gpt-oss). A frontier model with a 1M
context sees the same conversation at roughly **2%** full. Its `deep` cells were
never under the pressure the instrument was built to apply, so "deep 10/10" here
is a statement about headroom, not about robustness. **On the axis this
instrument is named for, the comparison is not like-for-like** - the tier
separates local arms from each other and cannot be repurposed as a frontier
comparator without rebuilding it against a context the frontier model would
actually strain.

**Both of the frontier arm's failures were SHALLOW**, which is the opposite of a
depth-degradation pattern and is consistent with the headroom reading.

### Where this leaves H0

Two instruments run, and **neither separates the frontier arm from gpt-oss-120b**:
L3-hard 12/12 vs 12/12, held-out depth 18/20 vs 18/20. That is now a pattern
rather than a single saturated tier, and it is the substantive H0 result so far -
on this lab's document-reasoning instruments, at these sizes, no measurable gap.
What it is not is evidence of equality: the sample sizes make a gap of tens of
percentage points invisible, exactly as AMENDMENT 2 registered.

Evidence: `results/raw/e66-20260819-opus-subagent-heldout.json`,
`results/raw/e66-20260819-opus-subagent-heldout-answers.jsonl`.


## E67 - PREREGISTRATION: the H6 deterministic-date arm (2026-08-19)

**Registered BEFORE any run.** Written after building `tools/date_calc.py` and
`tools/run_h6_date_arm.py` and after reading the statutory rules, but before a
single model call. No arm has been run at the time of writing.

### The hypothesis and its two-sided falsifier

> **H6: Delegating deterministic subproblems to deterministic tools improves task
> reliability more cheaply than allocating additional model reasoning to them.**

Falsifier, as registered in the R&D programme's AMENDMENT 2: H6 is rejected if
tool delegation **fails to convert the known arithmetic failures**, OR if it
**introduces more new failures than it removes**. Both directions are counted;
neither is reportable alone.

### Design

Six L4 questions whose answer is a date - `P1 P2 P3 B1 N1 N2` - asked single-turn
against the L4 pack. Two conditions, same model, same session, same prompts
except that the treatment appends a four-line notice that date tools exist:

| condition | tools offered |
|---|---|
| control | no |
| treatment | yes - `add_period`, `last_day_of_month`, `date_diff` |

Single-turn rather than the E57 conversation, deliberately: this isolates the
arithmetic from the depth confound. **The consequence is that these scores are
NOT comparable to E63/E66's held-out numbers**, and the comparison that matters
is within-experiment, control against treatment on the same model.
